text: The pass defense is sinking the season. Arizona is 1–4 at −54 and allows 32.4 points per game, the most in the league, after a 45–21 home loss to Detroit in which the defense gave up 412 yards and +0.33 EPA per play. It is 31st against the pass and 29th on defense overall, and even the run defense slipped from 2nd to 8th. The offense is 16th in EPA per play: 21st through the air and 15th on the ground.
DVOA has Arizona 24th (−11.2%), down from 19th. The offense is 13th and special teams 13th, but the defense ranks 28th.

A one-back offense (88% of plays; league 74%) with the 6th-most tight ends on the field, and play action on just 17% of dropbacks, 3rd fewest. The defense plays the 4th-fewest defensive backs and the 8th-most linebackers, and blitzes on 25% of dropbacks (9th lowest). Neither rush plan works: +0.32 EPA per dropback with four rushers (league +0.10) and +0.49 with five or more (league −0.01).

Arizona moves before the snap on 59% of plays (12th; league 58%) but is worse when it does: −0.09 EPA per play with motion against +0.09 without. The run game shows it most (−0.18 after motion, +0.25 without). The defense sees motion on 65% of plays (6th most) and holds up against it (+0.02), but without motion it is the worst in the league at +0.31, and +0.55 per dropback.

Jacoby Brissett is 23rd of 37 qualifiers at 0.00 EPA per dropback, with 9 touchdowns and 5 interceptions. Against Detroit he threw for 292 yards and 3 touchdowns and pushed the ball further (9.9-yard average depth of target, his season high). He still completes 5.5 points above expectation with the 4th-quickest release (2.6 seconds). Blitzes are the problem: −0.34 EPA per dropback when opponents send extra rushers against +0.15 when they don't.

Neither back is beating Next Gen Stats' expectation. Jeremiyah Love has 245 yards at 3.7 per carry (−0.39 over expected, 29th of 42 qualifiers) and −0.08 EPA per carry, and Tyler Allgeier 3.4 per carry (−0.16, 25th) at −0.18 EPA. The backs get 2.1 yards before contact (24th). Arizona has 10 broken tackles (2.0 per game, tied for 21st), 4 of them by Allgeier.

Trey McBride is still the focal point: 29% of the targets, 42 catches for 308 yards and 3 touchdowns, +0.29 EPA per target. Michael Wilson draws 37% of the air yards yet averages 5.6 yards per target at −0.14 EPA. Kendrick Bourne (17 of 22, +0.40 EPA per target, 1.0 yard after catch over expectation) remains the efficient option, and Elijah Higgins has caught all 8 of his targets for 96 yards.

Pass protection is about average: pressure on 21% of dropbacks (12th lowest) and a 5.6% sack rate (12th), though Detroit had 5 sacks. Elijah Wilkinson and Hjalte Froholdt have played every snap, Isaac Seumalo 99% and Paris Johnson 79%, with Jon Gaines and Isaiah Adams sharing the fifth spot. The interior run game is still the leak: 44 runs up the middle average 2.9 yards at −0.17 EPA, while runs off the left and right end average 5.4 and 6.3.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. FTN charged none of Detroit's 5 sacks to Brissett: three came on extended plays, one on a blitz and one when a standard rush won. Of 12 sacks this season, 5 were extended plays, 4 standard rushes that won, 2 his fault and 1 a blitz. He turns 26% of pressures into sacks, right at the 27% league average.

The run defense is still good (−0.14 EPA per rush, 8th), but the pass rush is the thinnest in the division by volume at 6.4 pressures per game (tied for 28th). It finishes well when it gets there: 11 sacks and a 7.1% sack rate (11th). Budda Baker has 2.5 sacks from safety, Walter Nolen, Josh Sweat and Darius Robinson have 5 pressures each, and eight other players have at least one.

Still the weak spot, 31st in EPA per dropback allowed. Budda Baker has allowed 241 yards and 3 touchdowns on 22 targets (114 passer rating), Mack Wilson 180 yards on 17 targets (134), and Denzel Burke 2 touchdowns (101) with an interception. Andrew Wingard remains the exception, with an interception, a forced fumble, 3 tackles for loss and a 67 rating allowed.

PFR's charting matches the EPA. Arizona has allowed a 109.1 passer rating (30th; league 92.4) and 8.7 yards per target (31st): 88 of 152 for 1,323 yards, 14 touchdowns (tied for most) and 3 interceptions. Opponents complete only 58% of those throws (7th lowest), but the catches are big ones. Linebackers have fared worst (117.5 rating on 44 targets, 30th among linebacker groups), and the safeties give up 12.6 yards per target.

Now average (13th in special teams DVOA, down from 4th). Chad Ryland is 8 of 10 on field goals with a 60-yarder and 12 of 12 on extra points. Blake Gillikin nets 38.0 yards per punt with 7 of 25 inside the 20, and Jalen Brooks (26.3) and Devin Duvernay (27.2) both average over 26 yards per kickoff return.

The two-game surge stalled in a 30–23 home loss to Baltimore, leaving Atlanta 2–3 with a −3 point differential. The offense was flat (−0.02 EPA per play, a 34% success rate) and slipped to 20th in EPA per play and 11th in success rate, though the run game is still 3rd in EPA per carry. The bigger change was on defense: the run defense fell from 1st to 15th in EPA per rush, and the unit is now 12th overall (from 8th). Giveaways (9) still outnumber takeaways (4).
DVOA slid back with the loss: Atlanta is 18th overall (from 15th). The offense holds at 17th, the defense dropped to 12th (from 8th), and special teams are still 27th.

A run-first offense (30th in pass rate over expected) that keeps about 1.6 tight ends on the field, 7th most. Two-back looks make up 23% of plays (league 20%) and have produced +0.16 EPA per play, against −0.12 with one back (29th). The defense rushes four on 72% of dropbacks and blitzes on 27% by FTN's count (22nd); four rushers (+0.03 EPA per dropback) and five or more (−0.03) have been about equally effective.

Motion still carries the passing game. Atlanta motions on 62% of plays (9th; league 58%), and dropbacks with motion are at −0.04 EPA against −0.25 without, the 7th-biggest passing gain in the league (2nd last week). Runs do as well without it as with it (+0.07 EPA either way). On defense, Atlanta sees motion on 51% of snaps (30th) and is excellent against runs without it (27% success rate allowed, 1st), but runs after motion gain 4.8 yards a carry (28th).

Michael Penix Jr. is still one of the league's most efficient passers at +0.30 EPA per dropback (6th of 37 qualifiers), with 3 touchdowns, 1 interception and a 104.8 passer rating. Baltimore was his toughest start: 19 of 32 for 240 yards and a touchdown, completions 5.8 points below expectation (Next Gen Stats) and three sacks, which pulled his season figure to 0.5 below expectation. He gets the ball out fast, 2.55 seconds on average (2nd quickest). Cooper Rush (−0.67 on 46) and Jack Strand (−0.60 on 19) keep the team at 27th in passing EPA. Play action remains the better call (+0.19 EPA per dropback on 37 against −0.21 without).

Bijan Robinson is among the best backs in the league: 580 yards at 5.7 per carry (3rd of 42 qualifiers), 1.7 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation (3rd) and a 50% success rate (2nd). With Pro Football Reference's New Orleans and Baltimore charting added, his 10 broken tackles (7 on runs) rank 5th. Brian Robinson remains an efficient change of pace, +0.09 EPA per carry on 51 carries. Bijan's receiving is still low value, 18 catches for 152 yards and a touchdown at −0.35 EPA per target.

Drake London is the passing game: 27 catches on 36 targets for 488 yards, +0.85 EPA per target, 44% of the team's air yards and 2.1 yards after the catch above expectation (7th of 118). Jahan Dotson gets the deep looks (16.3-yard average depth of target, 8th) but has caught 8 of 17 for −0.61 EPA per target. Kyle Pitts has 10 catches for 109 yards and a touchdown, with 3.4 yards of separation, and Austin Hooper has a touchdown among his 5 catches.

The protection numbers are the best in the league: pressure on 17% of dropbacks, the lowest rate of any team. The 7.3% sack rate (26th) is about the quarterbacks more than the line; see Who owns the sacks. Bergeron and Neuzil have played every snap, Lindstrom 94% and Jawaan Taylor 92%, with Jake Matthews at 85%. Runs outside either end remain the best plays (9.1 yards per carry on 21 to the left end, 8.3 and an 80% success rate on 15 to the right), while runs behind right guard average 2.9 with a 19% success rate.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It points at the quarterbacks. Cooper Rush turned 5 of 8 pressures into sacks (63%, 2nd highest; league 27%), and Penix is now at 4 of 11 (36%, 8th highest). FTN charged all three of Penix's sacks against Baltimore to him, two after he left the pocket, all against a four-man rush. Of Atlanta's 11 sacks, FTN put 4 on the quarterback, 3 on a standard rush, 3 on blitzes and 1 on an extended play.

The run defense fell to 15th in EPA per rush (−0.09) after Baltimore, though it is still the league's best against light boxes (−0.31 EPA per run with six or fewer in the box). The rush gets there without finishing: 12.2 pressures per game ranks 5th, but the 4.9% sack rate is 23rd. Cameron Thomas and Samson Ebukam each have 11 pressures, with 10 and 9 QB hits; Ebukam and Za'Darius Smith have 2.5 sacks each, Smith with 4 tackles for loss in 78 snaps.

11th in EPA per dropback allowed. The touchdowns are still concentrated in two players: Mike Hughes has allowed 18 catches for 283 yards and 3 touchdowns (121 passer rating), and Jessie Bates III 4 touchdowns on 17 targets (131). C.J. Henderson has been the steadiest corner, with 6 passes defensed and an 85 rating allowed on 36 targets, and Avieon Terrell has allowed 4 catches on 11 targets. Xavier Watts has the unit's interception and a forced fumble.

Atlanta allows a 98.6 passer rating in coverage (21st; league 92.4). Opponents complete 61.4% of charted targets (14th) for 6.8 yards per target (9th), but have scored 12 touchdowns against 1 interception (28th and tied for 28th). Safeties are hit hardest: a 124.0 rating (28th) and 6 touchdowns on 48 targets. The corners are at 90.9 on 100 targets and the linebackers at 90.8, helped by Harold Perkins (12 of 22 for 95 yards).

Still a weak spot, 27th in special teams DVOA, and its 2.2 special teams penalties per game rank 30th. Nick Folk is 9 of 12 on field goals with a long of 51 and perfect on 12 extra points. Jake Bailey nets 40.1 yards per punt with 8 of 17 inside the 20, and Zachariah Branch averages 11.9 yards on punt returns.

4–1 after a 30–23 win at Atlanta with Tyler Huntley at quarterback. The offense slipped from 3rd to 6th in EPA per play but is still 2nd in success rate, 5th passing and 5th rushing, scoring 29.2 points per game. Against Atlanta the run game carried it (+0.23 EPA per carry) while the passing game went negative (−0.12 per pass play). The defense gave back some of last week's jump, falling from 10th to 14th in EPA per play, and the point differential is +27.
DVOA has Baltimore 6th (20.6%), down one spot. The offense holds at 3rd (20.0%), the defense fell from 12th to 16th (−2.1%), and special teams improved from 25th to 21st.

Baltimore runs more than its situations would predict (9 points below expected pass rate, 4th lowest) and has the 2nd most tight ends on the field (1.7 per snap). The defense plays more defensive backs than any team (5.1 on average), so opponents see a light box on 60% of runs (3rd most; league 45%). Sending five or more rushers (−0.04 EPA per dropback) still edges the four-man rush (+0.01), and Baltimore blitzes at about the league rate (32%, FTN; league 31%).

Baltimore motions on 63% of snaps (7th; league 58%), and it keeps paying off in the run game: +0.16 EPA and 5.6 yards per run with motion (the best yards per carry in the league) against −0.14 and 3.8 without, the 4th-biggest motion gain on runs. Passing is the reverse: +0.45 EPA per pass play without motion (2nd) against +0.11 with it, the largest drop-off of any team. On defense, Baltimore is 7th against motion (−0.07 EPA per play) and 5th against passes with motion (−0.06).

Lamar Jackson didn't throw a pass in Week 5, but his season still ranks among the best: 3rd of 37 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.38), six touchdowns, one interception and completions 7.1 points above expectation (2nd by NGS). Tyler Huntley went 24 of 32 for 201 yards and two touchdowns at Atlanta, but on very short throws (4.8-yard average depth, 3.2 yards short of the sticks), and FTN charged him with three sacks; he is at −0.07 EPA per dropback on 47 dropbacks. As a team, play action (27% of dropbacks, 8th most) has been worth +0.41 EPA against +0.17 without.

Derrick Henry has 476 yards on 113 carries (4.2 per carry), slightly above Next Gen Stats' expectation (+0.2 yards per carry, 16th of 42 qualified backs), with 262 of those yards after contact. His EPA per carry is just below break-even (−0.05) with a 43% success rate. Justice Hill has been the efficient change-up: 133 yards on 18 carries (7.4 per carry) and +0.22 EPA per carry, best among the 68 runners with 15 or more carries. Henry has five broken tackles (four on runs) and Jackson four (Pro Football Reference charting), and the team has slipped from 10th to 17th in broken tackles per game.

Zay Flowers leads in yards (405 on 31 targets, +0.84 EPA per target) and adds 2.8 yards of YAC over expectation per catch, 5th among 118 NGS-tracked receivers. Mark Andrews matches him in volume (30 targets, 23%) but has 177 yards, −0.07 EPA per target and four drops on a 6.7-yard average depth. Rashod Bateman remains the downfield option (12.2-yard depth, +0.76 EPA per target), and Baltimore's nine drops are tied for 5th most (FTN).

Pass protection is still a strength, with pressure on 20% of dropbacks (7th lowest), but the sack rate has climbed to 6.9% (23rd) after four sacks at Atlanta, three of them charged to Huntley by FTN. Olaivavega Ioane and John Simpson have played every snap and Roger Rosengarten all but two, while Ronnie Stanley (76%), Jovaughn Gwyn (52%), Emery Jones (35%) and Carson Vinson (28%) share the rest. Runs average 2.7 yards before contact (12th), and runs off right end are still the most reliable at a 62% success rate. Linemen have drawn 15 accepted penalties, 27th in the league.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Jackson turns 29% of pressures into sacks, close to the league's 27% (16th highest of 40), and FTN charged none of his seven sacks to him. Week 5 was different: FTN charged three of the four sacks at Atlanta to Huntley, who turned three of his eight pressures into sacks. Of the team's 11 sacks, three came against blitzes, three on extended plays and two on a standard rush.

Pass rush volume is still below average (7.8 pressures per game, 21st; league 9.4), and the sack rate ranks 21st. Tavius Robinson leads with eight pressures, three sacks and seven QB hits, and Mike Green has seven pressures, two sacks and four tackles for loss in 46% of snaps. Trenton Simpson leads in tackles for loss (six). The run defense moved up from 21st to 16th in EPA per rush.

Pass defense slipped back from 7th to 15th in EPA per dropback. Roquan Smith (a 47 passer rating on 23 targets, an interception) and Trenton Simpson (51, an interception) still lead the coverage, Nate Wiggins has held 25 targets to 119 yards, and Kyle Hamilton has four passes defensed and an interception. Malaki Starks (12 of 13 for 168 yards and two touchdowns, a 158 rating) and Marlon Humphrey (237 yards on 25 targets) are where opponents have found yards.

Baltimore's 90.9 passer rating allowed ranks 15th (league 92.4), with 110 of 173 targets completed for 1,306 yards. Linebackers remain the strength at 47.5 on 43 targets with two interceptions (league 91.3 for linebackers). Safeties are still the weak spot at 117.1 and 10.5 yards per target (league 94.9 and 8.4), and corners have allowed 99.6 (league 93.0).

Tyler Loop is 9 of 11 on field goals with a 64-yarder and perfect on 15 extra points. Chris Moore averages 28.6 yards on eight kick returns, and Ryan Eckley nets 41.7 yards per punt with 10 of 19 inside the 20. Special teams moved up from 25th to 21st in DVOA.

Buffalo is 4–1 after a 37–34 win at the Rams on Monday night. The offense is now the league's best in EPA per play (+0.22), 2nd passing and 6th rushing, and is tied with Detroit for the league lead in scoring (32.8 per game). The defense keeps sliding: 30th in EPA per play and 28th in points allowed (28.2 per game) after giving up 454 yards in Los Angeles. Giveaways (9, against 5 takeaways) are the other blemish.
DVOA has Buffalo 3rd overall, up from 4th. The offense is 2nd, the defense 27th (from 26th), and special teams climbed from 7th to 4th.

Buffalo uses more tight ends than any team (1.8 on the field on average, league 1.4) and fewer running backs than any. One-back sets produce +0.23 EPA per play, and empty sets, used on 12% of snaps (double the league rate), have turned positive at +0.33. On defense, neither rush plan works: four rushers allow +0.21 EPA per dropback and five or more +0.33 (league +0.10 and about zero).

Buffalo motions on 63% of snaps (8th; league 58%), and after Week 5 it is the league's best offense with motion (+0.19 EPA per play, 1st) as well as 3rd without it (+0.26). Passes without motion are still the bigger weapon: +0.45 EPA and 9.6 yards per pass, 1st. On defense, motion makes no difference: +0.14 EPA per play allowed with it and +0.13 without, both near the bottom.

Josh Allen ranks 4th of 37 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.35), with seven touchdowns and four interceptions. At the Rams he threw only 19 passes, completing 12 for 210 yards with a touchdown and an interception. He throws into tight windows less often than almost anyone (32nd of 37), and his completions are 1.6 points over Next Gen Stats' expectation. Blitzes help him (+0.40 EPA when blitzed, +0.31 when not), and his 22 carries have a 68% success rate.

James Cook has 532 yards on 95 carries (5.6 per carry), 3rd in the league, and 1.0 yard per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation (8th of 42 qualified backs), with a 53% success rate. His seven broken tackles on runs are tied for 5th (Pro Football Reference charting, which doesn't yet include the Rams game). Buffalo leads the league in yards before contact per carry (3.5, league 2.5). Ty Johnson has caught all 10 of his targets for 131 yards.

Keon Coleman is the most efficient target: 15 of 18 for 224 yards and two touchdowns at +1.04 EPA per target. Dalton Kincaid has 277 yards on 21 targets with 2.3 yards of YAC over expectation (6th of 118). Khalil Shakir leads in targets (26) and separation (4.0 yards, 7th) on a short 5.9-yard average depth of target. DJ Moore draws 24% of the air yards on a 15.1-yard depth, and Josh Palmer has two touchdowns among his three catches.

Dion Dawkins, O'Cyrus Torrence, Connor McGovern and Alec Anderson have played every snap; Spencer Brown is at 85%, with Tylan Grable filling 51 snaps. Run blocking is still the league's best by yards before contact, and runs behind left guard average 5.3 yards at +0.38 EPA. The sack rate is 6.1% (18th) and pressure comes on 22% of dropbacks (17th, through Week 4). Anderson has four of the line's 12 accepted penalties, three for holding.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. The blame still splits. FTN charged three of Allen's 10 sacks to him, including the only one at the Rams, which came outside the pocket; one more came on an extended play. Four came against a standard rush and two on blitzes. Through Week 4 he turned 30% of pressures into sacks (league 27%).

Through Week 4 the rush produced 13.8 pressures per game, 2nd in the league (league 9.4), but the sack rate has fallen to 22nd. Gregory Rousseau has 6 of the team's 11 sacks, 17 QB hits, 22 pressures, eight tackles for loss and three forced fumbles. Bradley Chubb adds 1.5 sacks and seven QB hits, and Deone Walker four tackles for loss and four passes defensed. The run defense ranks 23rd in EPA per rush.

Pass defense ranks 28th in EPA per dropback. Through Week 4, Christian Benford (116.0 rating) and Maxwell Hairston (100.6) had each allowed two touchdowns on 20 targets, and C.J. Gardner-Johnson (47.5, one interception) was the bright spot. Opponents have made seven interception-worthy throws (tied for 6th most; league average 4.9). The defensive backs have 12 accepted penalties, the most of any secondary.

Through four games (the Rams game isn't charted yet), Buffalo allows a 103.3 passer rating in coverage (25th; league 92.4): 93 of 149 for 1,160 yards, 10 touchdowns and two interceptions. Cornerbacks see 54% of targets (league 46%) and allow 101.9 (25th). Linebackers are the weakest group at 112.0 (27th), with Dorian Williams allowing two touchdowns on 11 targets. Safeties are at 92.3 (13th).

Tyler Bass is 9 for 9 on field goals with a long of 49, but 15 of 17 on extra points. Greg Dortch averages 26.3 yards on 16 kick returns and Ray Davis 32.1 on seven. Tommy Doman Jr. nets 45.7 yards on 10 punts, five inside the 20. Special teams rank 4th in DVOA.

Carolina had its bye in Week 5, so its numbers are unchanged and it sits at 2–2 with a +12 point differential; only the league ranks moved. The offense is still 8th in EPA per play and 4th in points per game (30.3), while the defense allows 27.3 per game (26th) and has slipped to 21st in EPA per play (from 19th) as other teams played. Carolina is +3 in turnovers (7 takeaways, 4 giveaways), and both wins came with no giveaways.
DVOA keeps Carolina 9th overall through the bye. The offense moved up to 9th (from 11th) as others played, the defense slipped to 21st (from 18th), and special teams (5th) remain the best unit.

A pass-first, three-receiver offense: 2.5 wideouts per snap (tied for 10th) and 2nd in pass rate over expected. Empty backfields (8% of plays, league 6%) have produced +0.63 EPA per play (5th), and the two-back looks used on only 10% of snaps (league 20%) are at +0.18. The defense plays plenty of extra defensive backs (4.9 per snap, 6th most) and sends five or more on 36% of dropbacks, which has worked better than four rushers (−0.01 EPA per dropback against +0.11).

Carolina uses less motion than most (55% of plays, 20th; league 58%) but makes it count through the air: dropbacks with motion are at +0.31 EPA (3rd), against +0.14 without. Runs gain nothing from it (−0.12 with, −0.09 without). The defense is the problem against motion, allowing +0.07 EPA per play with it and −0.02 without; runs after motion average 5.5 yards against Carolina (31st) compared with 3.9 without.

Bryce Young comes out of the bye 9th of 37 qualifiers at +0.23 EPA per dropback, with completions 5.1 points above expectation (Next Gen Stats), 9 touchdowns, 2 interceptions and a 100.0 passer rating. FTN has charted one interception-worthy throw all season, tied for the fewest in the league. Opponents rarely blitz him (24% of dropbacks, 30th), which suits him: he is at +0.25 EPA per dropback without a blitz (5th) and +0.17 against one. His best game was Week 4 against Detroit, 29 of 41 for 329 yards, 2 touchdowns and completions 8.5 points above expectation.

Chuba Hubbard is running 1.3 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation (4th of 42 qualifiers) at 5.0 yards per carry, with 7 broken tackles (5 on runs). He has also caught 10 of 11 targets for two touchdowns and +0.96 EPA per target. The backups have not helped: AJ Dillon (2.5 yards per carry, −0.56 EPA per carry) and Jonathon Brooks (3.3, −0.27) have combined for 26 carries. Carolina's 3.25 broken tackles per game are tied for 7th.

Tetairoa McMillan is the lead target, with 26 catches on 39 targets for 385 yards, two touchdowns, +0.41 EPA per target and a third of the team's air yards. Jalen Coker has been the most efficient (18 of 22, 222 yards, two touchdowns, +0.58 EPA per target) but had no targets in Week 4. Darren Waller has two touchdowns and 3.3 yards of separation, the most of any Panther, and Brycen Tremayne has added 115 yards on 9 targets.

Still a split verdict. Young is pressured on 34% of dropbacks, the highest rate in the league, but the 5.6% sack rate ranks 14th and the backs gain 2.9 yards before contact per carry, 6th best. The line also draws flags: 13 accepted penalties (30th), 8 of them false starts, with Robert Hunt charged with 5. Rasheed Walker, Hunt and Luke Fortner have played nearly every snap, with Monroe Freeling at 88%. Runs behind left tackle average 8.0 yards; runs up the middle (3.0 yards, −0.24 EPA per carry) and to the right tackle and end (1.5 yards on 13 carries combined) are where the ground game stalls.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It splits the blame. Young turns pressure into sacks far less often than average (17% vs. 27%, tied for 4th lowest of 40), so he escapes most of it, and FTN has charged none of his 10 sacks to him. But 6 of the 10 came against a standard four-man rush, which points at the line, and three more came on extended plays after he left the pocket.

The pass rush is tied for 10th in pressures per game (11.0), but the 4.8% sack rate is 25th. Princely Umanmielen leads with 9 pressures, 3 sacks and 3 tackles for loss in under half the snaps, and Jaelan Phillips has 8 pressures and 2 sacks. Run defense is 20th in EPA per rush, and runs against light boxes remain the weak spot: +0.14 EPA per carry, last in the league.

20th against the pass (from 17th) after the bye. Tre'von Moehrig has played 96% of the snaps and allowed a 59 passer rating, Lathan Ransom has allowed 2 catches on 11 targets, and Will Lee has 4 passes defensed with a 76 rating on a team-high 25 targets. The soft spots are Akayleb Evans (14 of 20 for 226 yards, 124 rating) and Jaycee Horn (108 rating). Devin Lloyd leads the defense with two interceptions from linebacker.

Still one of the better coverage units by passer rating, 84.5 allowed (10th; league 92.4), with opponents completing just 55.7% of charted targets (2nd lowest) for 7.5 yards per target (15th). The linebackers remain the strength, a 74.4 rating on 45 targets with all 3 interceptions (Lloyd 2, Bobby Okereke 1); the safeties are at 79.6 and the corners at 97.7 with 8.7 yards per target.

One of the league's better units (5th in special teams DVOA). Ryan Fitzgerald is 9 for 9 on field goals with a long of 53 but has missed 3 of 13 extra points. Sam Martin nets 43.2 yards per punt with 8 of 13 inside the 20.

One afternoon at Lambeau undid most of what Chicago had built. The 31–7 loss to Green Bay came with five turnovers, 246 yards of offense and −0.48 EPA per pass play, and it dropped the defense from 5th to 20th in EPA per play and from 3rd to 18th against the pass. The Bears are 3–2 with a +23 differential and still 5th in points allowed at 19.2 a game, but the offense has slid from 9th to 12th in EPA per play and the turnover margin is now −4. The run defense, 24th in EPA per rush, remains the softest spot.
DVOA took the Green Bay game hard: Chicago fell from 8th to 19th overall at −2.6%, with the offense 14th (+1.0%) and the defense from 6th to 20th (+2.2%). Special teams are 18th.

Chicago still plays through tight ends, 1.66 on the field on average (5th), with Colston Loveland at 85% of snaps and Cole Kmet at 61%. The defense sends five or more on 38.7% of dropbacks against a 31.4% league rate and is better for it, −0.06 EPA per dropback with five or more against +0.06 with four. Opponents keep loading the box against the run game: eight or more defenders on 12% of designed runs, and Chicago is at −0.60 EPA on those 20 runs.

Motion is still the best thing in the Chicago offense and it is still underused. The Bears motion on 51.7% of snaps (25th) and average +0.09 EPA per play with it against −0.05 without, a swing that ranks 7th, and their 51.1% success rate with motion is the best in the league. The running game is the clearest case: +0.17 EPA and 5.4 yards a carry with motion against −0.22 and 3.8 without, still the largest motion gain on the ground in football. The defense is on the wrong end of the same split, allowing +0.11 EPA against motion and −0.10 without, and +0.21 per dropback when the offense motions.

Week 5 was the first game the carousel cost Chicago anything. With Caleb Williams out a third straight week, Tyson Bagent went 12 of 21 for 87 yards and two interceptions, and Case Keenum 11 of 19 for 108 and one more with completions 11.0 points below expectation. Williams is still 5th among 37 qualified passers at +0.31 EPA per dropback; Bagent is 27th at −0.07 with no touchdowns and three interceptions, and Keenum 32nd at −0.10. Chicago faces the blitz on 40% of dropbacks, the highest rate in the league, and is still better against it (+0.20 EPA per dropback) than without it (−0.04).

Kyle Monangai did not add a carry in Week 5 and remains the more efficient back by a distance: 5.4 yards per carry on 60 carries, +1.17 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation (5th of 42 qualified backs) and +0.10 EPA per carry. D'Andre Swift is at 4.5 yards on 78 carries, essentially at expectation (−0.06, 21st) and −0.05 EPA per carry. The blocking holds up at 2.90 yards before contact per carry (8th), and Chicago is 4th in broken tackles per game at 3.8 (Pro Football Reference charting), with Swift's seven the most on the team.

Luther Burden III leads with 35 targets and 266 yards but is slightly below zero at −0.04 EPA per target. Rome Odunze carries the vertical role, 273 yards at 9.4 per target on a 14.2-yard average depth and 35% of the air yards, while winning only 2.2 yards of separation, 110th of 118 qualified receivers. Kalif Raymond is the efficient one again, 24 catches on 27 targets at +0.62 EPA per target with 4.0 yards of separation (8th). Loveland has the worst return of the regulars at −0.39 EPA per target, 110 yards on 23 targets.

Darnell Wright, Garrett Bradbury, Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson have played all 383 snaps, and Theo Benedet has the larger share at left tackle, 62% to Braxton Jones's 38%. The protection numbers held through the Green Bay game: 20.6% pressure allowed (8th), a 5.6% sack rate (13th) and only eight offensive line penalties, 7th-fewest. In the run game right guard is still the main lane, 41 carries at +0.14 EPA and 4.2 yards, while right tackle (−0.29 on 30) and left guard (−0.47 on 25) keep losing.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Green Bay got four in Week 5, taking Chicago to 11. Williams was pressured on 34% of his dropbacks but turned just 21% into sacks, below the 27% league rate; Bagent is pressured on only 14% and converts 40% of it. FTN charged its first Chicago sack to a quarterback, Bagent, at Lambeau; of the 11, four came on blitzes, four on standard rushes beaten (two of them by Green Bay) and two on extended plays.

Chicago is 15th in pressures per game at 9.6 against a 9.4 league average and 7th in sack rate at 8.0% with 12 sacks. Austin Booker has become the finisher, four sacks, five tackles for loss and two forced fumbles on 58% of snaps; Dayo Odeyingbo has nine pressures and three sacks and Montez Sweat eight and two. Devin Bush Jr. adds five tackles for loss from linebacker. The run defense is 24th in EPA per rush.

Pass defense EPA fell from 3rd to 18th in a week. Dillon Thieneman has played every snap and allowed 7 of 16 for 96 yards with an interception (37.5 rating); T.J. Edwards (56.8) and Devin Bush Jr. (58.3) are holding up underneath, and Malik Muhammad is at 75.8 on 25 targets with an interception and a sack. The corners are where it goes wrong: Jaylon Johnson has allowed 19 of 23 for 354 yards (133.2), and Tyrique Stevenson 197 yards and three touchdowns on 17 targets (139.0).

Chicago has allowed a 99.8 passer rating in coverage (22nd; league 92.4) and 9.2 yards per target, the most in the league, on 25.8 targets a game, with six touchdowns and three interceptions. The linebackers are 2nd in the league at 57.2 on 34 targets and the safeties are middling at 96.9 (17th). The cornerbacks are last in the league at 123.4, with 793 yards and four of the six touchdowns on 65 targets, 12.2 yards per target.

Cairo Santos is 7 of 9 on field goals with a long of 50 and 14 for 14 on extra points. Tory Taylor has a 44.3-yard net on 12 punts with four inside the 20. Zavion Thomas averages 25.9 yards per kickoff return and Kalif Raymond 10.3 per punt return. DVOA has the unit 18th, and its eight penalties (24th) stand out on a team that is otherwise the 6th-least-penalized in the league at 6.4 flags a game, and tied for the fewest penalty first downs given away.

3–2 after a 31–24 win at Miami in which the defense forced three turnovers and held the Dolphins to −0.05 EPA per play, ending a two-game run of positive EPA allowed. The offense ranks 10th in EPA per play and the defense 13th, and the pass defense is now 6th. Burrow's four touchdown passes drove a passing game that averaged +0.29 EPA per pass play in Week 5. The point differential is +19.
DVOA jumped Cincinnati from 11th to 5th (21.1%), just ahead of Baltimore. The offense rose from 10th to 7th (14.9%), the defense from 21st to 14th (−3.4%), and special teams are 11th.

Cincinnati passes more than any team relative to its situations (9 points over expected pass rate, 1st). The defense still blitzes less than anyone (16% of dropbacks, FTN; league 31%), and when it sends five or more the results have been the league's best (−0.39 EPA per dropback, 1st). The four-man rush, used on 81% of dropbacks, has given up +0.09. On offense, 14% of runs face a heavy box of eight or more (6th highest; league 9%), and those runs have averaged −0.37 EPA.

Cincinnati motions on 53% of snaps (24th; league 58%), and its offense is still much better without it: +0.18 EPA per play without motion (5th) against −0.03 with, a gap that ranks 29th. Passing shows the same split (+0.25 without vs. +0.03 with). On defense, motion has helped Cincinnati against the run (−0.12 EPA per run vs. +0.15 without, the 4th-biggest gain) and made little difference against the pass.

Joe Burrow ranks 15th of 37 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.15), with 11 touchdowns and three interceptions after throwing four touchdowns at Miami (23 of 32, 190 yards). He is accurate (4.7 points over expected completion rate by NGS, 9th) in a quick, short game: 2.6 seconds to throw (3rd fastest) and a 7.4-yard average depth of target. Blitzes and play action still hurt: −0.11 EPA per dropback when blitzed against +0.24 when not, and −0.05 on play action, which Cincinnati uses on only 17% of dropbacks (2nd least).

Chase Brown is averaging 3.5 yards per carry, 0.7 below Next Gen Stats' expectation (38th of 42 qualified backs), with −0.14 EPA per carry and a 37% success rate. Only 94 of his 246 yards have come after contact. He has eight broken tackles, six on runs and two after catches, tied for 8th in the league (Pro Football Reference charting), and the team ranks 19th in broken tackles per game. He is also heavily targeted (24 catches on 28 targets) but averages 4.4 yards per target and −0.39 EPA.

Tee Higgins still leads in volume: 43 targets (23%), 42% of the team's air yards and 423 yards at +0.58 EPA per target on a 13.2-yard average depth. Ja'Marr Chase has 289 yards and four touchdowns on 38 targets (+0.48 EPA per target). Mike Gesicki is the most efficient option, with four touchdowns on 17 targets and +0.99 EPA per target, and Dohnte Meyers gets 4.1 yards of separation, 6th among 118 NGS-tracked receivers.

Still the most stable line in the division: Orlando Brown Jr., Dylan Fairchild, Ted Karras and Dalton Risner have played every snap and Amarius Mims 98%. Burrow's quick release keeps the sack rate at 4.4% (7th lowest) while pressure arrives on 22% of dropbacks (16th). Run blocking ranks 18th in yards before contact (2.4 per carry), and runs off the tackles and ends (26 carries) have been negative in all four lanes. Fairchild has four accepted penalties, three for holding, part of 11 by the line (17th).

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Burrow converts 20% of pressures into sacks, below the league's 27% (tied for 8th lowest of 40), and he wasn't sacked at Miami. FTN charged two of his nine sacks to him and six came against a standard four-man rush, so the sacks that do happen lean toward protection.

Still a four-man rush that gets home: 11.4 pressures per game (7th; league 9.4) and the 4th-best sack rate (17 sacks). Jonathan Allen leads with 10 pressures, three sacks and four tackles for loss, Dexter Lawrence has nine pressures, three sacks and five tackles for loss, and Boye Mafe three sacks and five tackles for loss. Cashius Howell has eight pressures in 40% of snaps. The run defense ranks 19th in EPA per rush.

Pass defense climbed from 10th to 6th in EPA per dropback. Jordan Battle has three interceptions and a 62 passer rating allowed, Daxton Hill a 65 rating on 26 targets with five passes defensed, and DJ Turner five passes defensed. Linebacker coverage is still the leak: Demetrius Knight has allowed 18 of 23 for 205 yards (a 118 rating) and Barrett Carter 193 yards on 27 targets.

Opponents keep throwing at Cincinnati (183 charted targets, 7th most) and have piled up 1,396 yards, but they complete only 57% (6th lowest) and the 84.0 passer rating allowed ranks 9th (league 92.4), helped by five touchdowns (tied for 4th fewest). Safeties have tightened up (60.8 on 39 targets, with all three interceptions) and corners allow 80.2, while linebackers allow 101.3 on 52 targets (league 91.3).

Evan McPherson is 10 for 10 on field goals with a long of 58 and perfect on 14 extra points. Dohnte Meyers averages 27.2 yards on 16 kick returns, and Ryan Rehkow nets 39.8 yards per punt with nine of 16 inside the 20. Special teams rank 11th in DVOA, though the unit's nine accepted penalties rank 28th.

3–2 after a 17–12 loss at the Jets, Cleveland's worst offensive game of the season (−0.30 EPA per play, 198 yards, a 25% success rate). The offense fell from 16th to 26th in EPA per play, the run game is last (−0.32 EPA per carry), and Cleveland is now outscored by 19. The defense keeps it close: 16th in EPA per play and 5th against the pass after holding New York to −0.18 EPA per play.
DVOA has Cleveland 26th (−13.5%), down from 24th. The offense fell from 25th to 28th (−17.8%), but the defense improved from 16th to 11th (−5.6%). Special teams dropped from 8th to 19th.

Cleveland passes much more than its situations would predict (7 points over expected pass rate, 4th highest). Two-back sets (18% of snaps) remain costly at −0.29 EPA per play, 5th worst, while one-back sets are near break-even (−0.03). The defense plays light boxes against 63% of runs, the most in the league (league 45%), and blitzes on 25% of dropbacks (FTN; league 31%); the four-man rush allows +0.05 EPA per dropback and five or more −0.26 (5th best).

Cleveland motions on just 51% of snaps (28th; league 58%), but no team gains more from it on passes: +0.33 EPA per pass play with motion (2nd) against −0.16 without. Runs are bad either way but far worse without motion (1.8 yards per carry and −0.55 EPA, against 3.9 and −0.20 with). Overall, the +0.33 EPA per play gain from motion ranks 2nd. On defense, Cleveland allows +0.03 EPA per pass play against motion and −0.09 without.

Deshaun Watson has slid to 21st of 37 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.05) after going 15 of 33 for 155 yards against the Jets, 16.6 points below his expected completion rate. He has seven touchdowns and two interceptions, but his season completion rate over expectation (−5.7 by NGS) is now the lowest of any qualified passer, and his 10.4% sack rate is 2nd highest. Play action still hasn't helped (−0.13 EPA per dropback vs. +0.10 without), and blitzes, which he sees on 38% of dropbacks (6th most), make no difference (+0.05 either way).

Quinshon Judkins is still breaking tackles without finding room: 3.0 yards per carry, 0.5 below Next Gen Stats' expectation (33rd of 42 qualified backs), a 27% success rate and −0.27 EPA per carry. His eight broken tackles (six on runs, two after catches) are tied for 8th in the league (Pro Football Reference charting), and 109 of his 221 rushing yards came after contact. Cleveland ranks 29th in yards before contact per carry (1.8) and last in EPA per run, so most of the problem is up front.

Denzel Boston is the big-play threat: 45% of the team's air yards on a 17.0-yard average depth (5th deepest among 118 NGS-tracked receivers), 330 yards, three touchdowns and 3.3 yards of YAC over expectation (4th). Harold Fannin Jr. gets 5.3 yards of separation, the most of any tracked receiver, and has three touchdowns on 27 targets. KC Concepcion matches Boston's 29 targets but has 149 yards and +0.03 EPA per target, and Isaiah Bond has three drops on nine targets.

Cleveland has allowed 19 sacks, including eight at the Jets, and its 10.3% sack rate is the worst in the league; pressure arrives on 26% of dropbacks (6th highest). Austin Barber, Spencer Fano and Zion Johnson have played virtually every snap and Tytus Howard 89%, while Elgton Jenkins (79%) and Luke Wypler (21%) have shared center. Runs average 1.8 yards before contact (29th), and runs off left end have averaged 1.5 yards. Howard's five false starts lead a line with 14 accepted penalties (26th), and Cleveland's 49 accepted penalties are the most in the league.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Watson turns pressure into sacks more than most: 40% (6th highest of 40; league 27%). But FTN charged none of the eight sacks at the Jets to him: three came against blitzes, three on extended plays and two on a standard rush. For the season, five of his 19 are on Watson, six came against blitzes, four on extended plays and four on a standard rush.

Mason Graham still leads with four sacks and six tackles for loss in 40% of snaps, and Maliek Collins has seven pressures, 2.5 sacks and seven QB hits. Pressure volume is modest (8.2 per game, 19th; league 9.4), but the sack rate ranks 6th. The run defense has slid to 28th in EPA per rush. Front-seven players have drawn 12 accepted penalties, the most in the league.

Pass defense is up to 5th in EPA per dropback (from 14th). Grant Delpit remains the best cover player (a 50 passer rating, an interception and three passes defensed), and Mekhi Blackmon has held 18 targets to 91 yards. Denzel Ward has allowed only 13 catches on 30 targets but three touchdowns, while Ronnie Hickman has allowed four touchdowns and Myles Harden 263 yards.

Opponents complete only 56% of targets against Cleveland (4th lowest) and four interceptions are tied for 8th, but 11 touchdowns allowed rank 26th, leaving the passer rating at 89.7 (14th; league 92.4). Corners (90.6 on 95 targets), safeties (89.5 on 50) and linebackers (88.3 on 36) are all close to the league marks.

Andre Szmyt is 10 for 10 on field goals with a long of 56 but 7 of 8 on extra points. Corey Bojorquez nets 45.1 yards per punt with eight of 24 inside the 20, and Malachi Corley averages 26.0 yards on 13 kick returns. Special teams fell from 8th to 19th in DVOA.

Dallas is 2–3 after a 24–16 home loss to Tampa Bay in which it turned the ball over three times and forced none. The offense still ranks 7th in EPA per play and 6th in success rate at 27.6 points per game (7th), but the Tampa game was its first negative one (−0.03 EPA per play). The defense is last in both EPA per play and success rate and allows 27.2 points per game (25th). The turnover margin has slid to −3 (five giveaways, two takeaways).
DVOA has dropped Dallas from 13th to 20th overall. The offense is 5th, the defense is still 32nd, and special teams have slipped from 6th to 10th.

Dallas stays a three-receiver offense: one back on 81% of snaps (league 74%) at +0.11 EPA per play, 2.7 receivers on the field on average (league 2.4), and a pass rate 3.4 points above expected (6th). The defense rushes four on 69% of dropbacks and gives up +0.60 EPA per dropback on those snaps, against a league +0.10. Sending five or more has been far better (−0.03), yet FTN has Dallas blitzing on 27% of dropbacks (21st; league 31%).

Dallas motions on 51% of snaps (26th; league 58%) and is about the same either way: +0.11 EPA per play with motion and +0.15 without, both 8th. Runs after motion are the problem at 2.7 yards per carry (32nd) against 4.3 without. On defense, opponents motion on 69% of snaps (3rd most) and average +0.29 EPA per play when they do (32nd) against −0.03 without (12th), the 2nd-largest gap in the league behind the Rams.

Dak Prescott is at +0.20 EPA per dropback (11th of 37 qualified), with completions 3.0 points above expectation and nine touchdowns against three interceptions. Week 5 was his roughest game: 24 of 42 for 316 yards, a touchdown, two interceptions and completions 6.0 points below expectation. The same soft spots remain: +0.06 EPA per dropback against the blitz vs. +0.26 without, and +0.09 on play action vs. +0.22 without. He gets the ball out quickly (2.70 seconds, 6th fastest) and is the 4th most aggressive passer into tight windows.

Javonte Williams has 74 carries at 3.7 yards per carry, 0.1 below Next Gen Stats' expectation (23rd of 42 qualified) and break-even by EPA (−0.01). Blocking is about average at 2.5 yards before contact per carry (14th; league 2.5). He has three broken tackles on runs, and the team has 13 in all, 14th per game, five of them by Ryan Flournoy after the catch (Pro Football Reference charting). Williams has also caught 17 of 20 targets for 94 yards and a touchdown.

CeeDee Lamb still has the best EPA per target (+0.76) of the 15 receivers with 40 or more targets, with 39 catches on 51 targets for 507 yards, four touchdowns and 38% of the air yards, though Tampa held him to two catches for 9 yards. George Pickens picked up the slack: 27 catches on 41 targets for 355 yards and his first touchdown (+0.40 EPA per target, 8th of the 15). Ryan Flournoy adds 1.6 yards after the catch over expected. Jake Ferguson has three touchdowns but −0.27 EPA per target on short looks, and FTN charts 11 drops for the team, tied for 2nd most (league 6.3).

Cooper Beebe, Tyler Booker, Terence Steele and Tyler Guyton have played nearly every snap, and Tyler Smith (60 snaps) has started to rotate in at guard alongside T.J. Bass (82%). Pressure is 24.9% of dropbacks (22nd; league 23.1%), but Tampa didn't record a sack, so the sack rate improved to 2.9%, 2nd in the league. The line has only five accepted penalties, 2nd fewest. The run split is still lopsided: runs behind left tackle average 7.9 yards and +0.38 EPA, while runs behind right tackle average 0.9 yards and −0.48 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. For Dallas it's a non-issue. Only 6 of Prescott's 52 pressures have become sacks (12% vs. a 27% league rate), 2nd lowest of 40 qualified quarterbacks, and he wasn't sacked in Week 5. FTN charged four of the six to him, with one rush won and one extended play.

The pass rush is the root of the defensive problem: 7.4 pressure credits per game (24th; league 9.4) and five sacks, a 3.1% sack rate that ranks 29th. Donovan Ezeiruaku leads with eight pressures, Rashan Gary has seven, and Quinnen Williams and Malachi Lawrence five each. The run defense has slipped from 16th to 22nd in EPA per rush, though Williams and Jaishawn Barham still have four tackles for loss apiece.

Dallas is last in pass defense EPA. DaRon Bland has allowed 21 of 29 for 284 yards and two touchdowns (a 126.2 rating), and Reddy Steward 12 of 13 for 186 yards and two touchdowns. Underneath, Barham has allowed 11 of 12 and Dee Winters 15 of 17. Shavon Revel (8 of 16, 65.4 rating) and Cobie Durant (1 of 5) remain the best corners, and Caleb Downs has two forced fumbles and a sack from safety.

Dallas has the worst coverage numbers in the league and is now the only team without an interception: a 124.3 passer rating allowed (32nd) and 74.8% completions (32nd). Cornerbacks are at 117.8 on 67 targets against a league 93.0. Linebackers have allowed 32 of 35 (117.1 rating), and safeties a 139.0 rating with three touchdowns on 29 targets (league 94.9).

Dallas ranks 10th in special teams DVOA. Brandon Aubrey is 9 of 12 on field goals with a long of 60 and 13 of 14 on extra points. KaVontae Turpin averages 27.4 yards on 20 kickoff returns and 11.1 on punt returns. Bryan Anger has punted 10 times, seven inside the 20, with a 43.8-yard net.

3–2 with a −14 point differential after a 23–17 win at the Chargers that the defense won: 3 takeaways, 5 sacks, 237 yards allowed and −0.40 EPA per play, the second-best defensive game of Week 5. The offense is still the problem at 25th in EPA per play, 27th in success rate and 19.4 points per game (26th). The defense is 15th in EPA per play overall, 4th against the pass but 29th against the run.
DVOA has Denver 16th overall, down from 14th. The defense climbed from 14th to 10th, the offense fell from 15th to 19th, and special teams rank 12th.

Denver is still a one-back offense (80% of snaps); two-back looks (16%) are at −0.09 EPA per play. It sees light boxes more than most (55% of runs against six or fewer, 6th) and has done little with them (−0.17 EPA per carry). The defense blitzes on 38% of dropbacks (7th; league 31%), but five or more rushers allow −0.01 EPA per dropback on 70 plays, no better than four-man rushes (−0.07). Runs into eight-man boxes have gashed Denver for +0.57 EPA per carry on 18 plays.

Denver motions on 59% of plays (14th; league 58%). Passes are a bit better with it (−0.06 EPA per dropback against −0.13 without), but runs after motion succeed only 32% of the time (31st) against 59% without (3rd). On defense the split is stark: with motion, offenses gain 4.4 yards per play (3rd); when they line up still they gain 7.6 (32nd), including 7.1 yards per carry and +0.24 EPA on runs (both 32nd).

Bo Nix is at −0.10 EPA per dropback (30th of 37 qualifiers) and completing 4.1% below Next Gen Stats' expectation (36th). His average intended target is 6.0 yards downfield, 3.0 yards short of the sticks, and FTN has charted 7 interception-worthy throws (tied for 6th-most; league average 4.9) to go with 6 touchdowns and 3 interceptions. At the Chargers he went 16 of 27 for 123 yards. The blitz still hurts him (−0.27 EPA per dropback when blitzed against +0.01).

J.K. Dobbins has 64 carries at 3.6 yards per carry, −0.16 EPA per carry and a 33% success rate, 0.76 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation (40th of 42 qualifiers). Denver's running backs still have no broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference), and the team's 4 broken tackles in five games rank last per game. RJ Harvey has caught 20 of 22 targets and averages 3.7 yards on 15 carries.

Jaylen Waddle leads with 31 targets and 35% of the air yards, catching 18 for 204 yards with 3.8 yards of separation (13th of 118 qualifiers), but has 3 drops. Courtland Sutton is still the drag: 11 catches on 25 targets, 4.2 yards per target and −0.43 EPA per target, with 2.7 yards of separation. Tight end Evan Engram has 10 catches for 121 yards and a touchdown on 17 targets, and Pat Bryant (9 of 12, 133 yards, +1.03 EPA per target) remains the most efficient wideout.

The same five linemen (Bolles, Powers, Wattenberg, Meinerz, McGlinchey) have played essentially every snap. Nix is pressured on 21% of dropbacks (11th) and sacked on 3.5% (4th); the Chargers got him once. Run blocking is the weak spot at 2.2 yards before contact per carry (22nd; league 2.5): left guard runs work (5.2 yards, 62% success on 13), but left tackle runs don't (−0.43 EPA on 9). Garett Bolles has 4 of the line's 9 accepted penalties.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Nix rarely lets pressure become a sack (17% vs. 27% league; tied for 4th-lowest of 40), and he has been sacked twice since Week 1. FTN charted his 6 sacks as 3 standard rushes, 1 blitz, 1 extended play and 1 charged to him; the Week 5 sack was a standard rush.

Zach Allen is still the engine: 14 pressures, 4 sacks, 13 QB hits and 4 tackles for loss. Nik Bonitto now has 3 sacks and 7 pressures after a big day against the Chargers. Denver's sack rate rose to 13th (13 sacks), but pressure volume is middling (8.2 credits per game, tied for 19th; league 9.4), and the run defense is 29th in EPA per rush allowed.

4th in pass defense EPA, up from 15th. Talanoa Hufanga has allowed 6 catches on 15 targets for 73 yards with 2 interceptions and a 16.1 rating, and Brandon Jones also has 2 interceptions but has given up 161 yards on 14 targets. Patrick Surtain II has allowed 9 of 18 with no touchdowns (68.5). Riley Moss has allowed 3 touchdowns but has an interception and 5 passes defensed, and Ja'Quan McMillian has given up 178 yards on 17 targets.

Denver has allowed a 79.9 passer rating in coverage (6th; league 92.4), with opponents completing 59% (8th) for 7.1 yards per target (10th). The safeties have 4 of the 5 interceptions and a 54.3 rating allowed. Linebackers see 32% of the targets (50), led by Alex Singleton (26, 84.1 rating), and the cornerbacks have allowed 4 of the 6 touchdowns with a 94.9 rating.

Wil Lutz is 8 of 11 on field goals with a long of 52 and 7 of 7 on extra points. Jeremy Crawshaw averages 48.9 yards per punt (45.3 net) on 24 punts, 12 inside the 20. RJ Harvey averages 29.2 yards per kickoff return and Marvin Mims Jr. 14.2 per punt return. DVOA ranks the unit 12th.

The 45–21 win at Arizona made Detroit the highest-scoring team in the league at 32.8 points a game, tied with Buffalo, and the offense is now 3rd in EPA per play, 3rd against the pass and 4th in success rate. Nothing changed on the other side: the defense is still 31st in EPA per play and allows 29.6 points a game (29th), though Week 5 was its least bad day since the opener at +0.02 EPA per play. That nets out to 3–2 and a +16 differential, propped up by a +4 turnover margin built on a single giveaway in five games.
DVOA has Detroit 15th overall at +3.9%, with the offense 10th (+10.1%) and the defense up from 30th to 25th (+10.5%). Special teams jumped from 13th to 6th (+4.2%).

The offense lives in one-back sets, 81% of snaps at +0.21 EPA per play, and the small two-back package (49 plays) has been even better at +0.25; empty is still a dead end at −0.61 on 13 plays. Play action comes on 31.9% of dropbacks, 3rd-most in the league, though it is worth nothing extra (+0.28 EPA per dropback with it, +0.29 without). On defense the rush count still does not matter: +0.25 EPA per dropback against four rushers and +0.21 against five or more. Opponents have dropped back 242 times against Detroit, more than against any other defense.

Detroit is still one of the few offenses that is better standing still: +0.22 EPA per play without motion against +0.14 with it, a gap that ranks 22nd, and the passing game drops from +0.39 to +0.19 when a man moves. It motions on 50.9% of snaps, 27th. The running game goes the other way, +0.07 EPA and 4.8 yards a carry with motion against −0.05 and 4.3 without. The defense is beaten either way, +0.16 EPA per play against motion (30th) and +0.14 without, on a league-average 57.4% motion rate faced.

Jared Goff is 7th among 37 qualified passers at +0.28 EPA per dropback, with 12 touchdowns, still no interceptions and a 111.3 passer rating. Arizona was one of his best days, 19 of 30 for 271 yards and three touchdowns, a 125.8 rating and his deepest average target relative to the sticks all year (+2.0 yards). His season completion rate is 0.9 points above expectation, and he is much better blitzed (+0.42 EPA per dropback) than not (+0.22).

Jahmyr Gibbs is the backfield: 105 carries at 4.8 yards, +0.52 yards per carry over Next Gen Stats' expectation (13th of 42 qualified backs) and +0.04 EPA per carry, plus 27 catches for 243 yards and two touchdowns on 34 targets. His 11 broken tackles (Pro Football Reference charting) are 4th in the league, on 132 touches, the heaviest workload in the top 10. The blocking is among the best at 3.08 yards before contact per carry (4th), and the team's rushing EPA has climbed to 8th.

Amon-Ra St. Brown has the volume without the efficiency: 57 targets (30% share), 37 catches, 372 yards and five touchdowns, but 6.5 yards per target and 0.58 yards of YAC below expectation, 105th of 118 qualified receivers. Sam LaPorta is the most efficient regular at +0.85 EPA per target with 3.6 yards of separation (21st) and three touchdowns. Jameson Williams scored his first two touchdowns of the year and is now at +0.71 EPA per target on a 16.8-yard average depth (6th-deepest), with 32% of the air yards, though he still has four of the team's seven drops. Isaac TeSlaa has 187 yards on 19 targets with 3.9 yards of separation (12th).

Penei Sewell, Juice Scruggs and Tate Ratledge have played 99% of the snaps, Blake Miller 81% at the other tackle, and left guard is still split among Christian Mahogany (62%), Ben Bartch (38%) and Larry Borom (29%). The protection is excellent, 18.9% pressure allowed (5th) and a 5.3% sack rate (11th). Runs up the middle are the most-used lane by far, 42 carries at 3.5 yards and a 52% success rate, and right end (+0.49 EPA on 11) is the most productive. The discipline is the problem: 15 offensive line penalties (27th), nine false starts, five of the flags on Miller.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Goff is pressured on 18.9% of dropbacks, 5th-lowest, and turns 28.2% of that into sacks against a 26.6% league rate. Arizona got three in the first quarter of Week 5, one blitz and two standard rushes beaten. Of the 11, FTN charged four to Goff (all at Buffalo in Week 2), four were standard rushes beaten and three came on blitzes.

The pass rush is the one working part of this defense: 12.6 pressures per game (4th; league 9.4), 20 sacks, the most in the league, and an 8.3% sack rate (5th). Aidan Hutchinson has 15 pressures, 11 QB hits and four sacks on 89% of snaps; D.J. Wonnum has five sacks on 56%; Alim McNeill has 10 pressures, 3.5 sacks and four tackles for loss; Derrick Barnes has three sacks and an interception. The run defense is 21st in EPA per rush, better than it was but still giving ground.

29th in pass defense EPA. D.J. Reed has allowed 316 yards and two touchdowns on 28 targets (126.5), Roger McCreary 266 and two on 32 (104.4) with seven passes defended, Avonte Maddox 158 and two on 11 (139.2), and Thomas Harper 128 on eight (145.8). Chuck Clark (53.6, an interception and a forced fumble) and Derrick Barnes (56.5) are the two who have held up, and Keith Abney II has allowed 3 of 6 with an interception.

Detroit has allowed 1,883 coverage yards, the most in the league, on 47.0 targets a game, with 14 touchdowns (30th), a 100.7 passer rating (23rd) and three interceptions. Every group is below average: cornerbacks 97.9 (22nd), safeties 104.9 (20th) and linebackers 102.4 (23rd). Jack Campbell is the most-targeted defender on the team, 22 of 33 for 257 yards and three touchdowns, and the linebackers have now allowed as many touchdowns as the cornerbacks, five each.

Jake Bates is perfect, 8 for 8 on field goals with a long of 54 and 20 for 20 on extra points. Jack Fox has a 43.3-yard net on 19 punts with eight inside the 20. Jacob Saylors averages 26.0 yards per kickoff return and Tom Kennedy 24.8, with Kennedy adding 13.2 per punt return. The unit is 6th in DVOA and among the least penalized, four flags in five games (5th).

The 31–7 win over Chicago was Green Bay's best game of the season by a distance: +0.25 EPA per play on offense, −0.34 on defense, 430 yards gained and five takeaways without a giveaway. It moved the defense from 21st to 10th in EPA per play and to 3rd against the pass, and the offense from 25th to 18th. The Packers are 3–2 with a −8 differential and a +3 turnover margin, and the running game is still the anchor dragging on all of it, 31st in EPA per rush.

One week moved Green Bay from 27th to 17th in DVOA at −0.3%. The defense jumped from 24th to 8th (−8.1%) and the offense from 28th to 21st (−7.3%), while special teams slipped from 11th to 17th (−1.2%).

Green Bay is in one-back sets on 81% of snaps at −0.04 EPA per play. Play action rose to 20.3% of dropbacks, still only 26th in the league against a 24% average, and it is worth +0.51 EPA per dropback against +0.01 without, the clearest unused lever on the team. Opponents still invite the run, playing a light box on 59% of Green Bay's designed runs, and Green Bay is at −0.35 EPA on those 55 runs. The defense blitzes less than it did, 33.5% of dropbacks (13th), with no gain from the extra rushers (+0.02 EPA per dropback with five or more, −0.08 with four).

Green Bay finally leaned on motion, and the season numbers show why. The motion rate is up to 63.3% of snaps (6th), and the offense averages +0.06 EPA per play with motion against −0.17 without, a +0.22 swing that ranks 5th. The passing game gains 8.3 yards per play with motion (2nd) against 5.0 without, and runs go from 2.2 yards a carry to 3.8. On defense it faces more motion than anyone, 70.2% of snaps and 83.8% of opponent runs, and handles motion runs (−0.06 EPA) far better than static ones (+0.17).

Jordan Love's best game came against Chicago: 25 of 31 for 367 yards, two touchdowns, no interceptions, a 137.5 rating and completions 11.6 points above expectation. Over five games he is 18th among 37 qualified passers at +0.11 EPA per dropback with 10 touchdowns and three interceptions, but his completion rate is still 3.8 points below expectation, 34th of 37, and FTN has charted six interception-worthy throws. His receivers have dropped 13 passes, the most in the league. He still has the quickest release of any qualified passer at 2.51 seconds and is much worse blitzed (−0.10 EPA per dropback) than not (+0.25), on a 40% blitz rate faced, 2nd-highest.

The running game remains the worst part of the team. MarShawn Lloyd is at 2.8 yards per carry on 40 carries, −1.36 yards per carry against Next Gen Stats' expectation, last of 42 qualified backs, and −0.31 EPA per carry. Kaleb Johnson has five broken tackles on 27 carries (Pro Football Reference charting) but is at −0.44 EPA per carry; Chris Brooks is at 4.7 yards on 15. The blocking is the root of it: 1.84 yards before contact per carry, 31st in the league.

Christian Watson is having the best season of any receiver in the division: 26 catches for 474 yards and six touchdowns on 40 targets, 11.8 yards per target and +2.0 yards of YAC over expectation (9th of 118), on only 2.5 yards of separation. Matthew Golden leads in targets (44) and air yards (38%, on a 14.7-yard average depth) and is now efficient at +0.31 EPA per target with 397 yards, though four of the team's drops are his. Tucker Kraft is the short option at +0.23 EPA per target and 3.3 yards of separation, and has three drops of his own.

Jordan Morgan and Sean Rhyan have played all 314 snaps, Anthony Belton 79% and Jacob Monk 59%, and five more linemen have taken at least 20% of the snaps in the remaining spots. Pressure comes on 24.0% of dropbacks (20th) and the sack rate is 5.1% (9th), helped by how fast Love throws. In the run game only right tackle is even (+0.01 EPA on eight carries); the middle, the most-used lane with left tackle at 22 carries each, is at 2.3 yards and −0.46 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Love is pressured on 24.0% of dropbacks and turns 21.3% of it into sacks, below the 26.6% league rate. Chicago got two in Week 5, both standard four-man rushes beaten. Of the 10, four were Minnesota blitzes in Week 1, three FTN charged to Love himself and three were standard rushes beaten.

A steady rush rather than a dominant one: 10.0 pressures per game (13th; league 9.4) and 14 sacks at a 7.5% rate (9th). Lukas Van Ness has nine pressures, eight QB hits and 2.5 sacks; Edgerrin Cooper has three sacks, six tackles for loss and an interception from linebacker; Devonte Wyatt has two sacks and a forced fumble on 49% of snaps; Dani Dennis-Sutton has six pressures in a 43% role. Zaire Franklin has played 99% of the snaps. The run defense is 25th in EPA per rush.

3rd in pass defense EPA, up from 21st. Xavier McKinney now has three interceptions and a 74.4 rating allowed on 13 targets; Evan Williams has played every snap and allowed 10 of 21 for 102 yards (58.0) with an interception, five pressures and a sack. Keisean Nixon still takes the most volume, 23 of 37 for 201 yards with no touchdowns (65.3), and Javon Bullard is at 72.1. Brandon Cisse remains the soft spot, 194 yards and two touchdowns on 17 targets (142.8) on 92% of snaps.

Green Bay has allowed a 77.0 passer rating in coverage, 3rd in the league, with seven interceptions, tied with Seattle for the most of any defense, 6.6 yards per target (6th) and only 1,058 yards (6th fewest). It concedes the short stuff (63.8% completions, 19th) and wins on the rest. The safeties are the strength at 53.9 on 55 targets (3rd) with four interceptions, the linebackers are 11th at 77.0 and the cornerbacks 15th at 93.5.

Trey Smack is 7 of 10 on field goals with a long of 59 and 9 of 11 on extra points. Daniel Whelan has been both busy and excellent: 22 punts, a 45.1-yard net and 14 inside the 20. Skyy Moore averages 16.0 yards per punt return and 27.5 per kickoff return, and Bo Melton 27.3 on kickoffs. The unit is 17th in DVOA. The team's penalties are still a drag: 46 for 369 yards, 9.2 a game (29th), 73.8 yards a game (27th) and 13 first downs given away (27th).

Houston finally won, 26–3 at Tennessee, and the defense did it: −0.39 EPA per play, 187 yards allowed and two takeaways. That one game moved the defense from 22nd to 11th in EPA per play, and it remains 3rd in success rate. The offense is 14th in EPA per play, but the run game is still 26th. At 1–4 the point differential is only −2.
DVOA has thought more of Houston than its record all season, and the win at Tennessee pushed it from 17th to 11th overall (10.7%). The offense is 11th, the defense 9th and special teams 22nd.

Still a one-back offense (79% of snaps, league 74%), and runs into seven-man boxes, 51% of designed runs, have cost −0.27 EPA each. On defense Houston fields the fourth-most defensive backs in the league (4.98 per snap, league 4.73) and blitzes on just 19.9% of dropbacks (31st; league 31.3%). The four-man rush now holds offenses to +0.01 EPA per dropback on 160 plays, against a league mark of +0.10.

Houston uses presnap motion on 57% of plays (19th; league 58%), and it still matters more here than almost anywhere. With motion the offense averages +0.11 EPA per play against −0.13 without, the 4th-largest gain in the league, almost all of it through the air (+0.26 vs. −0.12 per pass play, 3rd-largest). Runs with motion are still poor at −0.23 EPA per carry (28th). On defense Houston has seen motion on 48% of snaps, the fewest in the league, and its run defense against motion is the league's best at −0.33 EPA per run.

C.J. Stroud went 26 of 34 for 261 yards and a touchdown at Tennessee, completing 13.1% above expectation by Next Gen Stats, his second straight game above +13%. He is now at +0.13 EPA per dropback (17th of 37 qualifiers) and 6.7% CPOE (3rd), with 6 touchdowns and still no interceptions. He got the ball out faster in Week 5 (2.74 seconds, his quickest game) but still averages 2.96 for the season (league 2.88). Play action (+0.33 EPA per dropback on 45 plays vs. +0.05 without) and the blitz (+0.47 when blitzed vs. +0.02 when not) are where he does his damage.

The run game still isn't working. David Montgomery is at 2.7 yards per carry and −0.35 EPA per carry on 52 carries, 0.43 yards per carry below Next Gen Stats' expectation (31st of 42 qualifiers). Woody Marks has been the better back (3.5 yards per carry, −0.14 EPA, right at expectation) and now plays more snaps (53% to 46%). Houston has 9 broken tackles in five games (Marks 4 and Montgomery 3 on runs, Jared Wayne and Nico Collins 1 each after the catch), tied for 24th per game in Pro Football Reference charting.

Dalton Schultz and Xavier Hutchinson share the team lead with 31 targets each (18%). Schultz has turned his into 24 catches for 244 yards at +0.30 EPA per target with 3.8 yards of separation, while Hutchinson draws the most air yards (24% share) but has caught only 16. Nico Collins remains the most dangerous: 19 catches on 25 targets, 249 yards, 3 touchdowns and +0.75 EPA per target despite 1.9 yards of separation. Jaylin Noel has added 227 yards on 13 catches (+0.63 EPA per target) and gains 1.1 yards after the catch over expected.

Pass protection improved: pressure is down to 20.7% of dropbacks (9th), though the 6.9% sack rate is still tied for 21st. Four linemen have played every snap, and Ed Ingram has taken the larger share of right guard from Wyatt Teller (58% to 42%). The run-blocking problem has spread beyond the right side: runs behind left guard, right guard and right tackle (55 carries combined) each average −0.36 to −0.41 EPA, while runs up the middle and off left tackle are positive.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Stroud is pressured less than average (20.8% vs. 23.1%) but turns pressure into sacks more often (33% vs. 27%). FTN has still charged none of his 14 sacks to him: 9 came against a standard rush and 5 on extended plays, including one of each at Tennessee. That points at protection first, with his long time to throw as a factor.

The pass rush had its best day of the year at Tennessee, and 18 sacks on 200 dropbacks is now a 9.0% sack rate, 3rd in the league, on 11.4 pressures per game (tied for 7th). Will Anderson leads with 16 pressures, 7.5 sacks, 14 QB hits and 10 tackles for loss, and Danielle Hunter has 14 pressures and 3 sacks. Sheldon Rankins has 2 sacks and Jadeveon Clowney 1.5 in part-time snaps. The run defense ranks 9th in EPA per rush.

The pass defense climbed from 25th to 16th in EPA per dropback after holding Tennessee to −0.43 per pass play. Kamari Lassiter is still the most-targeted defender (23 of 32 for 280 yards, 108.9 rating) and has 6 accepted penalties, the most on the team, including 3 pass interference calls. Derek Stingley Jr. has been better (11 of 26, 81.9 rating), while Reed Blankenship has allowed 21 of 29 for 272 yards and two touchdowns. Blankenship and linebacker Jake Hansen have the only interceptions.

Coverage is now about league average: a 93.6 passer rating allowed (19th; league 92.4) and 7.3 yards per target (12th), with 6 touchdowns and 2 interceptions on 176 targets. Opponents still throw at the safeties far more than usual (41% of targets, league 23%), and the safeties have allowed a 99.9 rating. The cornerbacks are at 97.7 on 59 targets (league cornerbacks 93.0).

Ka'imi Fairbairn is 11 of 12 on field goals with a long of 58 and perfect on 11 extra points. Kai Kroeger averages 48.0 yards per punt (42.9 net) with 8 inside the 20. Jaylin Noel (25.7 yards on 11 kickoff returns), Woody Marks (24.3 on 7) and Tremon Smith (22.8 on 8) share kickoffs. DVOA ranks the unit 22nd, and Houston's 12 accepted special-teams penalties are still the most in the league.

Indianapolis fell to 2–3 with a 22–34 loss at Pittsburgh, where the defense gave back its Week 4 progress by allowing +0.24 EPA per play and 354 yards. Over five games the Colts rank 2nd in EPA per rush but 30th passing, and the defense is 26th in EPA per play and now last against the run. They remain the league's least-penalized team at 5.0 accepted flags per game, tied with San Francisco.
DVOA has Indianapolis 21st overall (−6.5%), down one spot from 20th. The offense is 20th and the defense 24th, with special teams (2nd) still the clear strength.

The Colts lean on play action more than most (29.6% of dropbacks, 6th; league 24.2%) and play more tight ends than average (1.56 per snap, league 1.44). Two-back looks are 16% of snaps and have produced +0.28 EPA per play, against −0.10 with one back, and runs into seven-man boxes are still positive (+0.11 EPA on 52% of runs). On defense Indianapolis blitzes on only 20.0% of dropbacks (30th; league 31.3%), and it makes little difference: four rushers and five or more have both allowed +0.12 EPA per dropback.

Indianapolis uses presnap motion on 62% of plays (11th; league 58%), and the offense is a bit better with it: −0.02 EPA per play with motion against −0.09 without (11th-largest gain). Motion runs remain the best part of it at +0.12 EPA per carry (3rd), while the passing game is poor either way and worse without motion (−0.30 EPA per pass play, 31st, vs. −0.10 with it). On defense the Colts have struggled against the run with or without motion (+0.05 and +0.12 EPA per run, 30th and 28th).

Daniel Jones threw 44 times at Pittsburgh, completing 24 for 267 yards with no touchdowns or interceptions and 3.8% below expected completion rate by Next Gen Stats. For the first time this season his average throw went past the sticks (+2.4 yards), but for the year it still lands 1.3 yards short. He is at −0.16 EPA per dropback (34th of 37 qualifiers) and −1.7% CPOE (28th), with 3 touchdowns and 4 interceptions, and FTN has charted 8 interception-worthy throws, tied for 3rd most (league average 4.9). Play action helps a little (−0.09 EPA per dropback with it, −0.19 without).

Jonathan Taylor carries the load: 101 carries for 3.9 yards per carry, +0.03 EPA per carry and a 41% success rate. He is still running below Next Gen Stats' expectation (−0.25 yards per carry, 27th of 42 qualifiers), and contact comes early: the team's 1.8 yards before contact per carry ranks 30th (PFR), so 190 of his 398 yards have come after contact. Indianapolis has 12 broken tackles in five games, tied for 17th per game (Taylor 5 rushing and 2 receiving, Seth McGowan 3 on 17 carries).

Tyler Warren is now the most-targeted player (36 targets, 22% share) with 30 catches, 213 yards and two touchdowns, but his average target is just 4.1 yards downfield and he has three drops. Josh Downs is still the best weapon: 34 targets, 30% of the team's air yards, 249 yards, +0.34 EPA per target and 1.1 yards of YAC over expected. Keenan Allen has 18 catches on 29 targets for −0.07 EPA per target, and Laquon Treadwell has 157 yards on 11 catches.

The same five linemen have played nearly every snap (Bortolini and Goncalves all of them, Nelson and Travis 99%, Raimann 98%), and the line has just 2 accepted penalties, the fewest of any offensive line. They allow pressure on only 18.0% of dropbacks (4th) and a 4.8% sack rate (8th). Every running lane except right guard (9 carries, −0.16 EPA) has produced positive EPA, led by left end (+0.35 on 10 carries) and the middle (+0.17 on 27).

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Jones is pressured well below average (18.0% of dropbacks vs. 23.1%) and converts pressure to sacks right at the league rate (26.5% vs. 26.6%). FTN charted his 9 sacks as 3 standard rushes, 3 blitzes, 2 extended plays (one at Pittsburgh) and 1 charged to him.

The pass rush is still thin: 6.8 pressures per game is tied for 26th and the 5.4% sack rate is 20th. DeForest Buckner leads with 8 pressures, 4 sacks, 8 QB hits and 4 tackles for loss, Adetomiwa Adebawore has 2 sacks in part-time work (34% of snaps), and Laiatu Latu has 6 pressures and a sack. The run defense has fallen to 32nd in EPA per rush, though heavy boxes still stuff opponents (−0.30 EPA per run on 14 runs).

Pass defense is 23rd in EPA per dropback. Charvarius Ward remains the best of the group (7 of 18 for 111 yards, 60.2 rating), while Justin Walley (21 of 30 for 241 yards) and Sauce Gardner (13 of 22 for 244 yards, 112.7 rating) have given up the most. Safety A.J. Haulcy has allowed only 6 catches on 21 targets, but for 218 yards and two touchdowns, and Camryn Bynum is at 121.4 on 16 targets.

The Colts allow 8.7 yards per target in coverage (30th) and a 104.9 passer rating (28th; league 92.4), with 10 touchdowns and 1 interception on 175 targets. Linebackers have allowed 35 completions on 44 targets for 404 yards (118.2 rating), with Bryce Boettcher giving up 2 touchdowns on 9 targets, and safeties have allowed 4 touchdowns on 39 targets (120.4). The cornerbacks are the steadiest group at 97.5 on 76 targets (league cornerbacks 93.0).

Still a real strength. Spencer Shrader is 16 for 16 on field goals with a long of 58 (10 of 11 on extra points), Seth McGowan averages 29.1 yards on 14 kickoff returns, and Rigoberto Sanchez averages 51.7 yards per punt (46.6 net) with 6 inside the 20. DVOA ranks the unit 2nd.

Jacksonville is 4–1 after a 19–17 home win over Philadelphia, outgaining the Eagles 408 yards to 232 and holding them to −0.20 EPA per play. The Jaguars allow 14.0 points per game (2nd) with a +53 point differential, and rank 5th in offensive EPA per play, 3rd in defensive EPA and 1st against the run. The one soft spot in Week 5 was the ground game (−0.29 EPA per rush), which kept a 408-yard day to 19 points.
DVOA still ranks Jacksonville 2nd overall (30.1%), behind only San Francisco. The offense is 8th, the defense 3rd and special teams 20th.
