Jacksonville uses empty sets nearly twice as often as the league (11% of snaps, league 6%) and they keep working (+0.40 EPA per play on 32 plays), while its two-back looks (20%) average +0.20. It plays more tight ends than average (1.51 per snap, league 1.44). On defense it fields the fewest defensive backs in the league (4.14 per snap), and the blitz is still the weapon: five or more rushers have held offenses to −0.37 EPA per dropback on 58 plays, 2nd-best in the league, against +0.10 with four.

Jacksonville uses presnap motion on 62% of plays (10th; league 58%) and is efficient either way: +0.15 EPA per play with motion and +0.16 without, both top-10 marks. The defense is still better without motion (−0.14 EPA per play, 5th) than with it (−0.05, 11th), though the gap has narrowed since Week 4. Runs show it most clearly: −0.31 EPA per run without motion (2nd) against −0.16 with it.

Trevor Lawrence threw for a season-high 331 yards against Philadelphia (24 of 39, 2 touchdowns, 1 interception), but completed only 0.9% above expectation by Next Gen Stats, his lowest mark since Week 2. For the season he is at +0.28 EPA per dropback (8th of 37 qualifiers) and 5.2% CPOE (7th), with 10 touchdowns and 3 interceptions, getting the ball out in 2.72 seconds. The blitz is still the weak spot: +0.03 EPA per dropback when blitzed against +0.37 when not.

Bhayshul Tuten remains the lead back: 82 carries at 4.3 yards per carry and 0.29 yards over Next Gen Stats' expectation (15th of 42 qualifiers), down from 0.67 after Week 4. He does most of his work after contact (209 of his 349 yards in PFR charting), because the team averages only 1.9 yards before contact (28th). Chris Rodriguez Jr. has 113 yards on 28 carries. Jacksonville has 16 broken tackles in five games, tied for 9th per game (PFR), 9 of them Tuten's.

Parker Washington is the clear No. 1: 35 targets (26% share) and 41% of the team's air yards, turned into 22 catches, 352 yards, four touchdowns and +0.60 EPA per target. Jakobi Meyers remains the most efficient: 15 catches on 18 targets, two touchdowns and +0.99 EPA per target. Brenton Strange is a steady second option (21 of 26 for 235 yards, 3.3 yards of separation), Josh Cameron has two touchdowns on 12 targets, and Brian Thomas Jr. has 9 catches on 17 targets with three drops.

Protection is about average: pressure on 23.4% of dropbacks (19th) and a 6.4% sack rate (19th). Emmanuel Pregnon has played every snap, with Robert Hainsey, Ezra Cleveland, Cole Van Lanen and Anton Harrison at 90–97%. Penalties are the bigger problem: the offense draws 5.6 accepted flags per game, the most in the league, and the line's 15 includes 5 on Pregnon and 4 on Hainsey. The run game wins up the middle (+0.16 EPA on 30 carries) and around right end, while runs behind the right guard and right tackle are negative.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Lawrence now converts pressure to sacks at about the league rate (27.0% vs. 26.6%), down from 32% after Week 4. But FTN charged both of his Week 5 sacks to him, the first it has put on him this season; his 10 sacks are now 4 against a standard rush, 2 against a blitz, 2 on extended plays and 2 his own fault.

11 sacks on 198 dropbacks is a 5.6% sack rate (19th), on 11.0 pressures per game (tied for 10th). Josh Hines-Allen leads with 11 pressures, 1.5 sacks and 7 QB hits, Travon Walker has 10 pressures and 2 sacks, and Dennis Gardeck adds 4 QB hits in part-time snaps. The run defense is now 1st in EPA per rush (−0.22).

7th in pass defense EPA, and opponents keep giving the ball away: FTN has charted 10 interception-worthy throws against Jacksonville, tied with the Rams for the most in the league (league average 4.9). Jourdan Lewis and Foyesade Oluokun have 2 interceptions each, and Jarrian Jones and Travis Hunter 1 each. Jones has been targeted most (42 times, 21 catches, 293 yards, 62.9 rating), and Montaric Brown remains the soft spot at a 143.8 passer rating allowed.

The Jaguars allow a 79.2 passer rating in coverage (5th; league 92.4), built on 4 touchdowns allowed (tied for 2nd fewest) and 6 interceptions on 191 targets. The catch is still yardage, at 7.9 yards per target (25th). Cornerbacks, counting Travis Hunter, see 54% of targets and have allowed a 75.9 rating with four of the six interceptions, linebackers are at 70.7 on 55 targets, and the safeties have allowed 109.4 on 28.

Cam Little is 9 of 11 on field goals with a long of 57 and 12 of 13 on extra points. Logan Cooke averages 47.6 yards per punt (41.6 net) with 5 inside the 20. Ameer Abdullah (29.3 yards on 9 kickoff returns) and Josh Cameron (24.9 on 8) handle kickoffs. DVOA ranks the unit 20th, and its 2 accepted special-teams penalties are tied for 2nd fewest.

4–0 with a +41 point differential coming out of the Week 5 bye, the last unbeaten team in the division. Kansas City ranks 4th in offensive EPA per play, 1st in EPA per rush and 5th in success rate, and scores 29.5 points per game (5th). The defense moved back up to 7th in EPA per play while idle and allows 19.3 points per game (7th).
DVOA has Kansas City 4th overall (down from 3rd while on bye), with the 4th-ranked offense and the 15th-ranked defense (down from 10th). Special teams rank 15th.

Kansas City still leads the league in play action (36% of dropbacks, league 24%) and screens (18%, league 8%). Two-back looks (19% of snaps) are at +0.17 EPA per play, a bit better than one-back sets (+0.13). On defense the four-man rush holds offenses to −0.04 EPA per dropback (league +0.10), while blitzes with five or more have been hit for +0.09 on 45 plays (23rd). Kansas City is the only defense that hasn't put eight men in the box on a run.

Kansas City motions on 59% of plays (13th; league 58%) and is one of the few offenses that is better without it: +0.32 EPA per play without motion (2nd) against +0.08 with it. The gap is all in the run game, where runs without motion average 8.0 yards and +0.41 EPA (both 1st) and runs after motion 4.0 yards and −0.09. On defense, it has faced motion on 68% of plays (4th), and passes after motion have hurt (+0.11 EPA per dropback against −0.28 without, 3rd).

Patrick Mahomes is still playing fast and short: 2.70 seconds to throw (7th-fastest of 37 qualifiers), 7.1 intended air yards and tight-window throws on 8.6% of attempts (qualifier average 15.3%). He is at +0.21 EPA per dropback (10th), with 9 touchdowns, 2 interceptions and a 106.2 passer rating, completing 1.5% below Next Gen Stats' expectation (27th). Play action (+0.32 EPA per dropback against +0.14) and the blitz (+0.42 when blitzed against +0.12) both help him.

Kenneth Walker III is still the best runner in the league by Next Gen Stats: 87 carries for 537 yards, 6.2 yards per carry and 2.52 yards over expected per carry, first of 42 qualifiers and well clear of second (1.87). He still leads the league with 14 broken tackles (12 on runs) per Pro Football Reference and has 267 yards after contact. Kansas City is tied with the Chargers for the most broken tackles per game (5.0).

Travis Kelce is the most efficient regular target: 16 catches on 22 targets for 246 yards, 2 touchdowns, +0.74 EPA per target and 3.5 yards of YAC over expected (3rd of 118 qualifiers). Tyquan Thornton is the deep threat (17.4-yard average depth, 3rd, with 219 yards, 2 touchdowns and +1.27 EPA per target). Rashee Rice (13 of 17, 190 yards) gets 4.1 yards of separation, 4th in the league. Xavier Worthy is tied with Kelce for the team lead in targets (22) but is at 6.0 yards per target and −0.15 EPA per target.

Mahomes is pressured on 22% of dropbacks (14th) and sacked on 4.2% (5th). Creed Humphrey, Trey Smith, Kahlil Benson and Jaylon Moore have played nearly every snap, with Kingsley Suamataia (77%) and Mike Caliendo (25%) splitting the fifth spot. Kansas City averages 2.7 yards before contact per carry (11th). Outside runs carry the ground game: left end runs average 10.8 yards and +0.65 EPA, while the 42 runs up the middle average 3.2 yards at −0.15 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Mahomes turns pressure into sacks less often than most (19% vs. 27% league; 7th-lowest of 40). FTN charted 4 of his 6 sacks as a standard rush winning; the two in Week 4 were an extended play and a blitz.

The pass rush is still the weak spot: only 4 sacks and a 2.6% sack rate, tied with Miami for 31st. George Karlaftis III leads with 13 pressures and 10 QB hits but has no sacks. R Mason Thomas (8 pressures) and Felix Anudike-Uzomah (4 pressures) have one sack each. As a unit Kansas City averages 9.8 pressure credits per game (14th; league 9.4), and the run defense ranks 12th.

10th in pass defense EPA. L'Jarius Sneed is still targeted most (33) and has allowed 26 catches for 247 yards. Mansoor Delane has allowed 12 of 18 for 117 yards with an interception and 3 passes defensed, and Nohl Williams has 4 passes defensed with a 67.5 rating allowed. Kristian Fulton has allowed 13 yards on 7 targets with an interception, and the secondary's 9 accepted penalties are tied for 3rd-most.

Kansas City has allowed an 80.3 passer rating in coverage (8th; league 92.4), 6.6 yards per target (5th) and only 4 touchdowns (tied for 2nd-fewest), though opponents complete 64% of their throws (21st). The linebackers have been hardest to throw on (70.4 rating), led by Drue Tranquill (4 of 11 for 45 yards). The soft spots are Sneed (108.0) and the safeties Jaden Hicks (108.5) and Alohi Gilman (110.4).

Harrison Butker is 7 of 9 on field goals with a long of 46 and 13 of 13 on extra points. Matt Araiza averages 52.3 yards per punt (47.3 net) with 9 of 12 inside the 20. Emmett Johnson (28.5), Brashard Smith (26.6) and Nikko Remigio (25.0) share kickoff returns. The unit's 9 accepted penalties are tied for 3rd-most, and DVOA ranks it 15th.

The Rams are 2–3 with a −1 point differential, and Week 5 flipped their usual story. In a 37–34 loss to Buffalo they had no giveaways for the first time all season and the offense posted +0.25 EPA per play, but the defense allowed 436 yards and +0.28. Los Angeles is now 9th in EPA per play on both sides of the ball (the defense was 3rd a week ago), with 8 giveaways against 5 takeaways.
DVOA ranks the Rams 10th (10.8%), with the 6th-ranked offense and 7th-ranked defense. Special teams are still last at −15.3%.

One of the heaviest offenses: 1.7 tight ends per snap (3rd most) and the 3rd-fewest backs. It sees eight-man boxes on 15% of runs (league 9%), and those runs average −0.27 EPA; two-back looks (−0.17) and empty sets (−0.37 on 19 plays) still lose value. The defense plays the 2nd-most defensive backs and is far better sending extra rushers: −0.18 EPA per dropback with five or more against +0.06 with four.

The Rams use motion on 65% of plays (5th) and are worse with it: +0.04 EPA per play with motion against +0.14 without. On passes the gap is +0.08 against +0.20. The defense shows the biggest motion split in the league: offenses gain 0.42 EPA per play from motion against Los Angeles, because without it the Rams allow −0.29 (2nd best) and with it +0.12 (28th).

Matthew Stafford was sharp against Buffalo (40 of 54 for 383 yards, 3 touchdowns, no interceptions) and is now 16th of 37 qualifiers at +0.13 EPA per dropback, with 9 touchdowns and 6 interceptions. He completes 1.8 points above expectation. FTN has charted 11 interception-worthy throws for the offense, still the most in the league (average 4.9). Blitzes remain his problem: −0.14 EPA per dropback when opponents send extra rushers against +0.23 when they don't.

Kyren Williams is running well: 343 yards at 4.9 per carry, +0.60 yards over Next Gen Stats' expectation (11th of 42 qualifiers) and +0.03 EPA per carry, plus 27 catches for 200 yards. Blake Corum adds 4.8 per carry (+0.10 over expected). The backs get 3.0 yards before contact (5th). Broken tackles are scarce: 8 in four games charted by PFR (tied for 21st per game), 5 of them by Williams.

Davante Adams is the downfield target: 27 catches for 441 yards and 4 touchdowns on 45 targets, a 15.0-yard average depth of target, 37% of the air yards and +0.41 EPA per target. Puka Nacua matches him with 45 targets and has 337 yards and 1.7 yards after the catch above expectation (12th of 118). Tyler Higbee (20 of 25, 224 yards, +0.41) has been efficient. FTN has charged the offense with 10 drops, 4th most.

One of the best lines in football. Alaric Jackson, Steve Avila, Coleman Shelton and Warren McClendon have played every snap and Kevin Dotson 99%. Pressure comes on 18% of dropbacks (2nd lowest, through Week 4), the sack rate is 3.1% (3rd), and backs get 3.0 yards before contact (5th). Runs behind right guard (−0.54 EPA on 17 carries) are still the leak, while 46 runs up the middle average 5.2 yards.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. There have been seven, and FTN charged none to Stafford: three came when a standard rush won, two against blitzes and two on extended plays, including the only one against Buffalo. Through Week 4 he turned 20% of pressures into sacks, below the 27% league average.

Volume is still low: 7.8 pressures per game through Week 4 (22nd) and a 4.9% sack rate (24th), with 8 sacks. Byron Young leads with 3.5 sacks, 11 pressures, 6 QB hits and a forced fumble, and Omar Speights has 2 sacks. The run defense slipped to 13th in EPA per rush (10th a week ago).

12th in EPA per dropback allowed after Buffalo, down from 2nd. PFR's player charting doesn't include that game yet. Through Week 4, Trent McDuffie had allowed 7 catches for 42 yards on 21 targets (a 23 passer rating) with 7 passes defensed and an interception, and Quentin Lake had 7 passes defensed, an interception and a forced fumble (65 rating). Jaylen Watson (2 touchdowns, 135 rating) and Kamren Kinchens (2 touchdowns on 5 targets) were the soft spots.

PFR's charting still covers only the first four games. Through Week 4 the Rams allowed a 78.4 passer rating (4th; league 92.4) and 5.0 yards per target (1st): 68 of 122 for 615 yards, 7 touchdowns and 3 interceptions. Cornerbacks are the strength at a 62.7 rating (2nd among cornerback groups). Safeties see 35% of the targets (3rd most; league 23%) and allow a 96.6 rating.

Last in special teams DVOA. Harrison Mevis is 5 of 9 on field goals with a long of 48 and 14 of 14 on extra points, Ethan Evans nets 38.1 yards per punt, and Jordan Whittington averages 25.9 yards per kickoff return.

0–5 with a −45 point differential after a 17–23 home loss to Denver: 3 turnovers, 5 sacks allowed and −0.40 EPA per play, the offense's worst game of the season. It is last in EPA per play and passing EPA, 27th rushing, and scores 16.8 points per game (30th). The defense keeps them in games: 6th in EPA per play, 9th against the pass, 12th in sack rate.
DVOA ranks the Chargers 29th, up from 31st. The offense is still last (32nd), the defense 18th and special teams 28th.

The Chargers still run the heaviest backfield in the league: two or more backs on 38% of snaps (1st; league 20%), and they go empty on 9.5% (4th; league 6%). Only empty sets have worked (+0.11 EPA per play on 29); two-back looks are at −0.16 and one-back sets −0.30. They play the second-fewest tight ends (1.22 per snap) and pass the least of any team relative to expectation. On defense, extra rushers have been the answer: −0.26 EPA per dropback with five or more on 43 plays (6th), against +0.05 with four.

Los Angeles motions on 73% of plays (4th; league 58%), and almost nobody has gotten less out of it: −0.26 EPA per play after motion (31st) against −0.06 without. Passes after motion are at −0.30 EPA per dropback with a 35% success rate (both 31st). On defense the Chargers handle motion well (−0.15 EPA per play, 2nd) but allow +0.10 when offenses line up still (25th).

Justin Herbert is at −0.21 EPA per dropback (36th of 37 qualifiers), completing 2.8% below Next Gen Stats' expectation (32nd), with 5 touchdowns, 7 interceptions and a 70.2 passer rating. FTN has charted 10 interception-worthy throws, 2nd-most in the league (league average 4.9), and he is out of the pocket on 34% of dropbacks, the most of any offense (league 21%). Against Denver he went 14 of 24 for 121 yards. Play action is the only thing near break-even (−0.03 EPA per dropback against −0.28), and he is at −0.34 when blitzed.

Omarion Hampton has 9 broken tackles on runs (tied for 6th in the league in total broken tackles, Pro Football Reference) but is averaging 3.7 yards per carry and −0.26 EPA per carry, 0.49 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation (34th of 42). Keaton Mitchell is 41st (−0.81) at 4.1 yards per carry, though he has caught 12 of 14 targets. Kimani Vidal has been the best of the three on the ground (6.3 yards per carry on 14). The Chargers' 22 broken tackles on runs lead the league by 9, and they are tied with Kansas City for the most per game (5.0).

Tre Harris is the lead receiver: 15 catches on 25 targets for 225 yards, +0.22 EPA per target and 3.2 yards of separation. Ladd McConkey is still the most efficient (12 of 17, 183 yards, +0.63 EPA per target) but has no catches since Week 3. Quentin Johnston has caught 7 of 19 with 2 drops, and the tight ends are underwater: Oronde Gadsden II at −0.48 EPA on 16 targets and David Njoku at −0.63 on 8. The Chargers' 9 drops are tied for 5th-most.

The line is still the biggest problem: Herbert is pressured on 28% of dropbacks (30th) and sacked on 9.7% (31st), and Denver got him 5 times. The lineup keeps changing: only Jake Slaughter and Cole Strange have played nearly every snap, while Joe Alt (66%) and Rashawn Slater (76%) have missed time, with Trevor Penning (43%) and Travis Burke (38%) filling in. The line's 20 accepted penalties are the most in the league (Alt 6, Strange 4). The 40 runs up the middle have cost −0.35 EPA each; left guard (+0.28 on 11) and left tackle (+0.19 on 14) runs are the only ones clearly positive.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Herbert converts pressure to sacks at 35% (league 27%; 31st of 40). Week 5 swung back toward the protection: FTN charged none of Denver's 5 sacks to him (3 came on blitzes). For the season, 7 of his 17 sacks came against a blitz, 4 were charged to him (all in Week 4), 3 were extended plays and 3 standard rushes.

Khalil Mack leads with 10 pressures, 3 sacks and 5 tackles for loss. Tuli Tuipulotu has 9 pressures, 2 sacks, 7 QB hits, 2 forced fumbles and an interception, and Akheem Mesidor has 2.5 sacks. As a unit the Chargers average 8.6 pressure credits per game (tied for 17th; league 9.4) and rank 12th in sack rate with 11 sacks. The run defense ranks 14th.

9th in pass defense EPA. Cam Hart has allowed 206 yards on 19 targets but has an interception and 5 passes defensed, and Genesis Smith has 2 interceptions with 2 touchdowns allowed. Tarheeb Still has allowed 7 of 15 for 83 yards. Offenses are picking on the linebackers: Del'Shawn Phillips has allowed 10 of 10 (130.0 rating) and Daiyan Henley 10 of 14 for 101 yards.

The Chargers have allowed a 94.8 passer rating in coverage (20th; league 92.4), and opponents complete 67% of their throws (29th) for 7.6 yards per target (19th). The cornerbacks give up the most per throw (9.4 yards per target), and the linebackers have allowed 27 of 34 for a 102.1 rating. Tony Jefferson (118.3) is the most-beaten safety.

Cameron Dicker is 7 of 9 on field goals with a long of 42 and 9 of 9 on extra points. J.K. Scott averages 48.1 yards per punt (42.5 net) with 6 inside the 20. Kimani Vidal (25.6) and Keaton Mitchell (23.5) return kickoffs. DVOA still ranks the unit 28th.

3–2 with a +3 point differential after a 17–45 loss at New England in which the defense gave up 540 yards and +0.42 EPA per play, the worst defensive game of Week 5. That one game dropped Las Vegas from 4th to 19th in defensive EPA per play (22nd against the pass, 10th against the run). The offense is 13th in EPA per play: 10th passing, 29th rushing, and 26.4 points per game (9th).
DVOA dropped Las Vegas from 12th to 25th. The defense fell from 11th to 26th, the offense is 16th and special teams 14th.

Las Vegas is still a heavy team: two or more backs on 31% of snaps (3rd; league 20%) and the fewest receivers on the field (1.9 per snap; league 2.4), with 1.7 tight ends (4th). Two-back looks (+0.10 EPA per play) and empty sets (+0.28 on 17 plays) have beaten one-back sets (−0.06). The defense rarely blitzes (25% of dropbacks, 26th), and its four-man rush now allows +0.16 EPA per dropback on 134 plays, while five or more rushers hold offenses to −0.11 on 46.

Las Vegas motions on 59% of plays (15th; league 58%), down from 66% after Week 4. It lifts the passing game (+0.25 EPA per dropback after motion, 7th, against 0.00 without) but sinks the run game (−0.32 EPA per carry after motion, 31st, with a 29% success rate, 32nd). On defense it has faced motion on 66% of plays (5th) and handles it (−0.07 EPA per play, 6th); plays without motion are the problem, at 7.6 yards per play (31st) and +0.17 EPA (30th).

Kirk Cousins has been efficient: +0.16 EPA per dropback (14th of 37 qualifiers), 12 touchdowns, 4 interceptions, a 100.7 passer rating and 3.1% above Next Gen Stats' completion expectation (14th). At New England he went 19 of 28 for 243 yards and a touchdown. He still rarely leaves the pocket (12% of dropbacks, 5th-lowest; league 21%), and play action remains a big lever (+0.43 EPA per dropback against +0.06).

Ashton Jeanty is still stuck: 88 carries at 3.3 yards per carry, −0.28 EPA per carry and a 31% success rate, 0.17 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation (26th of 42). He has 6 broken tackles on runs and 8 in all (Pro Football Reference), and adds 22 catches for 215 yards and 2 touchdowns, though with 4 drops. Mike Washington Jr. averages 5.0 yards per carry on 25.

Brock Bowers has pulled ahead as the top target: 24 catches on 34 targets for 312 yards, 3 touchdowns and +0.51 EPA per target, despite only 2.4 yards of separation (103rd of 118 qualifiers). Jeanty has 30 targets, and Tre Tucker is the deep threat (14.3-yard average depth, 29% of the air yards, 274 yards). Michael Mayer has caught 21 of 25, and Cody White has 3 touchdowns on 14 targets.

Cousins is pressured on 26% of dropbacks (25th), and New England sacked him 3 times, though the 4.2% sack rate is still 6th. Jackson Powers-Johnson (74%) and Caleb Rogers (26%) share one guard spot; the other four linemen have played every snap. The run blocking is the bigger issue: 1.4 yards before contact per carry (32nd; league 2.5), every run direction is negative, and the 44 runs up the middle average 3.3 yards at −0.17 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Cousins rarely lets pressure become a sack (17% vs. 27% league; tied for 4th-lowest of 40). FTN charted his 8 sacks as 4 standard rushes, 3 charged to him and 1 extended play; in Week 5, two were standard rushes and one was charged to him.

Las Vegas averages 13.4 pressure credits per game, 3rd in the league (league 9.4). Maxx Crosby leads with 21 pressures and 13 QB hits, with 2 sacks. Malcolm Koonce leads in sacks (3), with Kwity Paye at 2 and Nakobe Dean at 1.5, for 13 sacks and a 10th-ranked sack rate. The run defense ranks 10th, and runs into eight-man boxes have been stuffed at −0.96 EPA per carry on 7 plays.

22nd in pass defense EPA, down from 5th. Hezekiah Masses has 3 interceptions and 6 passes defensed and has allowed a 67.8 passer rating on 22 targets, but also 2 touchdowns. Eric Stokes is the most-targeted defender (25 targets, 96.3 rating) and drew 2 pass interference flags for 51 yards at New England. Taron Johnson has allowed 15 of 23 for 159 yards, and linebacker Nakobe Dean 14 catches on 16 targets.

Las Vegas has allowed a 103.3 passer rating in coverage (24th, down from 12th; league 92.4) and 8.3 yards per target (28th). The cornerbacks still hold up: an 81.1 rating and 54% completions on 81 targets. The safeties are the soft spot at a 130.4 rating, 11.0 yards per target and 5 of the 11 touchdowns, with Isaiah Pola-Mao (2 touchdowns on 7 targets, 158.3) and Treydan Stukes (171 yards on 14 targets) the most beaten. Linebackers have allowed 28 of 35.

Matt Gay is 11 of 12 on field goals, his first miss of the season, with a long of 59 and 11 of 11 on extra points. AJ Cole averages 49.9 yards per punt (43.4 net) with 7 inside the 20. Dylan Laube averages 30.3 yards per kickoff return and Malik Benson 13.6 per punt return. DVOA ranks the unit 14th.

Miami is 0–5 after a 31–24 home loss to Cincinnati. The 24 points were a season high, but three giveaways undid it. The offense ranks 29th in EPA per play, 30th in success rate and 31st in scoring (14.0 per game). The defense is 28th in EPA per play and 30th against the pass, with the run defense (11th) the one strength. The −62 point differential is the league's worst by eight points.
DVOA has Miami 32nd overall at −47.1%, the only team below −40%. The offense is 31st, the defense 29th and special teams 31st.

Miami plays the fewest tight ends in the league (1.1 on the field on average) and the 5th most backs. Two-back looks take 29% of snaps (league 20%) and lose −0.21 EPA per play; one-back sets lose −0.10. On defense, the rush count hasn't mattered: four rushers allow +0.26 EPA per dropback and five or more +0.40.

Miami motions on 74% of snaps, 2nd most (league 58%), and it still hasn't worked. Plays with motion average −0.19 EPA (30th) and a 32% success rate (last), against +0.08 and 53% without (4th). Passes after motion average 4.7 yards against 8.5 without. On defense, opponents' passes after motion gain +0.36 EPA per play (31st) and 8.6 yards (32nd).

Malik Willis ranks 33rd of 37 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (−0.13), with two touchdowns and four interceptions after throwing two against Cincinnati (15 of 27, 137 yards, one touchdown). He throws deeper than any qualified quarterback (10.4-yard average depth of target), into tight windows 22% of the time (3rd highest), and holds the ball 3.16 seconds (3rd longest). Blitzes still hurt most (−0.35 EPA per dropback blitzed, −0.02 not), and play action no longer helps (−0.17 with it).

Ollie Gordon II is the lead back: 236 yards on 47 carries (5.0 per carry), 0.7 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (9th of 42), with +0.09 EPA per carry and five broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference charting), though only a 34% success rate. De'Von Achane averages 3.7 on 34 carries, 0.3 below expectation (28th). The run game has climbed to 20th in EPA per carry. Miami is 2nd in yards before contact per carry (3.4), but that is mostly Willis's own runs; the backs average about 2.5, the league rate.

Malik Washington draws 28% of targets and 32% of air yards (23 catches, 262 yards) at about break-even EPA per target (−0.01). Chris Bell runs the deepest routes of any NGS-qualified receiver (17.9-yard average depth of target) and is 2nd in YAC over expectation (+3.8), but has 5 catches on 15 targets. Kevin Coleman Jr. gets the least separation of 118 qualified receivers (1.5 yards) and has 36 yards on 17 targets. Greg Dulcich has caught 13 of 17.

Aaron Brewer, Austin Jackson, Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor have played every snap; Jonah Savaiinaea is at 84%, with Jarrett Kingston taking 48 snaps. Miami allows pressure on 28% of dropbacks (29th) and a sack on 8.8% (27th). Runs behind left tackle work (7.2 yards, +0.39 EPA), runs around left end don't (2.1 yards). The line has 12 accepted penalties: four on Jackson and three holds on Paul.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It still leans toward the quarterback, but less each week. FTN charged four of Willis's 14 sacks to him, all in Weeks 1 and 2, and three more came on extended plays. His pressure-to-sack rate (31%, league 27%) is 14th highest of 40. Week 5's three sacks split one standard rush, one blitz and one extended play.

Miami still has only four sacks, tied with Kansas City for fewest, and none came against Cincinnati; the sack rate ranks 31st. Pressure volume is 6.2 per game (30th; league 9.4). Chop Robinson leads with 11 pressures and six QB hits, and Zach Sieler has two sacks and five tackles for loss. The run defense is 11th in EPA per rush, down from 6th.

The pass defense is 30th in EPA per dropback. Chris Johnson has allowed three touchdowns on 23 targets (134.6 rating), Jason Marshall 15 of 18 for 184 yards, and linebacker Willie Gay Jr. all 11 targets for 128 yards and two touchdowns. Dante Trader is the exception, with an interception and a 41.7 rating. Opponents have made only two interception-worthy throws (league average 4.9).

Miami allows a 111.0 passer rating in coverage (31st; league 92.4), a 69.4% completion rate (30th) and 13 touchdowns on 160 targets. Linebackers rank last among linebacker groups at 122.0 and see 39% of targets (league 27%); Jacob Rodriguez has allowed three touchdowns on 30. Cornerbacks are 31st at 119.9. Safeties are the good group at 76.7 (9th), with two of the three interceptions (Michael Taaffe, Trader).

Special teams rank 31st in DVOA. Riley Patterson is 7 of 9 on field goals with a long of 41 and 5 of 6 on extra points, and had two kickoff penalties against Cincinnati. Jaylen Wright averages 27.9 yards on 12 kick returns. Bradley Pinion averages 45.5 yards gross and 39.6 net on 17 punts, six inside the 20.

5–0, the only unbeaten team in the division, and still built entirely on defense. Minnesota is 1st in defensive EPA per play, 1st against the pass, 2nd against the run, 1st in success rate and sack rate, and 1st in points allowed at 12.8 a game; New Orleans managed 142 yards in the 23–13 win. The offense is 28th in EPA per play and last in success rate at 35.7%, scoring 21.8 points a game. A +6 turnover margin and 259.8 yards allowed a game keep making up the difference.

DVOA moves Minnesota up from 10th to 7th at +19.5%: the No. 1 defense (−24.6%, up from 2nd) and the No. 1 special teams (+13.3%) carrying the 30th-ranked offense (−18.5%). The 29-place gap between offense and defense ranks is the widest in the league.

The offense uses extra backs more than most, two or more on 30% of snaps against a 20% league rate, and those looks are the only positive ones (+0.06 EPA per play, against −0.17 for one-back sets and −0.16 on 15 empty snaps). Play action comes on 30% of dropbacks (5th) and is worth a little, +0.04 EPA per dropback against −0.07 without. The defense is still the most aggressive in football by a distance, five or more rushers on 70.4% of dropbacks against a 31% league rate, holding offenses to −0.18 EPA per dropback when it sends extra and −0.26 when it rushes four.

Motion has started to help the offense: −0.02 EPA per play with it against −0.20 without, a +0.17 swing that now ranks 6th, almost all of it in the run game (−0.04 EPA with motion against −0.38 without, 3rd-largest gain). The motion rate is only 53.5%, 23rd. The defense is the bigger story: against static offenses it allows −0.36 EPA per play and 3.6 yards per pass play, both the best in football, but only −0.07 against motion, a gap that ranks 30th. Opponents still motion on just 52.9% of snaps against it (26th).

Kyler Murray put together his cleanest game at New Orleans, 24 of 30 for 229 yards and a touchdown with no turnovers, a 109.6 rating and completions 6.8 points above expectation. The shape has not changed, though: he did not attempt a single tight-window throw, and his average pass landed 4.1 yards short of the sticks. Over 122 dropbacks he is 29th of 37 qualified passers at −0.09 EPA per dropback with two touchdowns and two interceptions, while completing 3.8 points above expectation (11th). Minnesota is much worse against the blitz (−0.23 EPA per dropback) than without it (+0.09).

Aaron Jones is the run game, 97 carries at 4.2 yards with a 36% success rate, −0.40 yards per carry against Next Gen Stats' expectation (30th of 42 qualified backs) and −0.14 EPA per carry. Contact is still the problem: Minnesota has nine broken tackles in five games, 1.8 a game (24th), and Jones has four on 109 touches (Pro Football Reference charting). The blocking is average at 2.50 yards before contact per carry (15th), and Week 5 was the worst rushing day of the season at −0.37 EPA per carry.

Justin Jefferson is back in the offense and is again its best player: 19 catches on 24 targets for 258 yards and three touchdowns, +0.88 EPA per target and 1.3 yards of YAC above expectation (19th of 118), on 56% of the snaps. T.J. Hockenson still has the most targets (27) and catches (23) at +0.63 EPA per target and 3.4 yards of separation, though he is 111th of 118 in YAC above expectation. Jordan Addison holds the deep role (30% of the air yards, a 13.8-yard average depth) and has caught 11 of 22 at −0.10 EPA per target.

Blake Brandel has played every snap and Will Fries and Brian O'Neill 99%, with Christian Darrisaw at 67%, Donovan Jackson at 56% and Joe Huber at 44%. Pressure allowed has improved to 19.9% (6th), but too much still ends on the ground: 15 sacks on 169 dropbacks, an 8.9% rate that ranks 28th. On the ground right tackle (+0.10 EPA, 6.5 yards on 17 carries) and right end (+0.18 on eight) are the only positive lanes, and the two most-used, the middle (29 carries, −0.30) and right guard (28, −0.17), are still where the offense goes.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. By quarterback, Carson Wentz turned 6 of his 9 pressures into sacks, a 67% rate that points at protection; Murray is pressured on 20% of dropbacks and turns 36% into sacks, above the 26.6% league rate. Week 5 shifted the charting: both New Orleans sacks were charged by FTN to Murray. Of the 15, six were standard rushes beaten, four extended plays, three quarterback-caused and two blitzes.

The best pass rush in football: 14.0 pressures per game against a 9.4 league average, 17 sacks and a 9.5% sack rate, 1st in both pressures per game and sack rate. Dallas Turner has 22 pressures, 14 QB hits, 5.5 sacks and two forced fumbles, though he did not add to those totals at New Orleans; Andrew Van Ginkel has 10 pressures, four sacks and an interception with a 7.6 passer rating allowed in coverage; Blake Cashman has 10 pressures and 2.5 sacks from linebacker; Kyle Van Noy has six tackles for loss on 31% of snaps. The run defense is now 2nd in EPA per rush.

1st in pass defense EPA. Isaiah Rodgers has allowed 7 of 22 for a 31.4 rating with an interception, James Pierre 8 of 15 for 37.6 with another, and Byron Murphy has taken the most volume, 20 of 30 for 234 yards, and now has three interceptions with a 50.6 rating. Harrison Smith is at 52.8 on 11 targets. Safety is the one leak: Theo Jackson has allowed all three targets thrown at him for 98 yards and two touchdowns (158.3), and Josh Metellus is at 102.8 on 24.

Minnesota has allowed a 67.2 passer rating in coverage, the best in the league, with the fewest touchdowns (three), six interceptions (3rd) and a 57.1% completion rate (5th). The cornerbacks are the best group in the league at 40.5 on 67 targets, no touchdowns and five interceptions, and the linebackers are 3rd at 65.6. All three touchdowns have come against the safeties, who rank 23rd at 112.3.

Will Reichard is 15 for 15 on field goals with a long of 56 and 8 for 8 on extra points, which is most of why Minnesota is 1st in special teams DVOA. Myles Price averages 29.8 yards per kickoff return and 21.6 per punt return. Brett Thorson (13 punts, a 40.2-yard net, six inside the 20) and Johnny Hekker (12, 38.6, two inside the 20) are still splitting the punting. The team is the 3rd-least-penalized in the league at 6.0 flags a game, with one defensive back penalty all season, the fewest in the league.

New England is 3–2 after a 45–17 win over Las Vegas, its best game of the season by a wide margin: 540 yards and +0.42 EPA per play. That one game lifted the offense from 23rd to 11th in EPA per play, and the passing game is now 9th. The defense has slipped to 17th in EPA per play but is still 8th against the pass and 4th in points allowed (18.8 per game). The run defense (30th) and turnovers (11 giveaways, 6 takeaways) remain the weak spots.
DVOA has New England 13th overall, up from 26th. The offense jumped from 26th to 15th, the defense is 6th (from 7th), and special teams slipped to 23rd.

New England still plays two or more backs on 27% of snaps (league 20%), and those looks lose −0.32 EPA per play, against +0.17 in one-back sets. It uses fewer tight ends than most (24th). On defense, sending five or more rushers remains the better call (−0.14 EPA per dropback, against +0.04 with four), while runs into an eight-man box have gained +0.18 EPA per carry.

New England motions on 54% of snaps (21st; league 58%), and motion now helps the passing game: 7.6 yards per pass with motion (5th) against 7.3 without. The run game is still the problem. Runs after motion average 2.9 yards (30th), against 4.6 without (6th). On defense, runs after motion are held to −0.02 EPA, against +0.05 without.

Drake Maye had the best game of his season against Las Vegas: 26 of 34 for 374 yards, four touchdowns, no interceptions and a 150.9 passer rating. He has climbed to 13th of 37 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (+0.18), and his completions are 4.6 points over Next Gen Stats' expectation (10th). His seven interceptions are tied with Justin Herbert for the league lead. He holds the ball 3.06 seconds (5th longest), and play action still hasn't helped (−0.01 EPA per dropback with it, +0.23 without).

Rhamondre Stevenson has pulled ahead: 227 yards on 57 carries (4.0 per carry), 0.5 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (12th of 42 qualified backs), at −0.04 EPA per carry. TreVeyon Henderson averages 3.9 on 42 carries with a 33% success rate and −0.13 EPA. Stevenson broke the team's first two tackles on runs in Week 5 (Pro Football Reference charting), but New England still has the second fewest broken tackles on runs (2) and is tied for 28th in broken tackles per game (1.6).

Romeo Doubs leads in targets (23) and air yards (27%), with 219 yards and two touchdowns on a 16.6-yard average depth of target (7th of 118 NGS-qualified receivers). DeMario Douglas added 65 yards on five targets against Las Vegas and now has 147 yards, two touchdowns and 4.0 yards of separation (10th). Mack Hollins remains the most efficient (15 of 20 for 209 yards, +0.64 EPA per target), and Hunter Henry has 177 yards with 1.3 yards of YAC over expectation (18th).

Alijah Vera-Tucker has played every snap, with Jared Wilson (96%), Morgan Moses (93%) and Will Campbell (86%) close behind; Ben Brown has taken 163 snaps and four others have rotated in. The sack rate has improved again to 5.9% (17th), though pressure still comes on 25% of dropbacks (24th). Runs behind left tackle average 2.2 yards and behind right guard 3.2. Moses has five of the line's 13 accepted penalties (three false starts) and Campbell four.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It still points mostly at the line. Maye turns 24% of pressures into sacks, below the league's 27%. FTN charged two of his 11 sacks to him, the lone sacks in Weeks 4 and 5; six of the others came against a standard rush of four or fewer.

The pass rush is middle of the pack: 8.6 pressures per game (17th; league 9.4) and a sack rate that ranks 15th. Elijah Ponder added two sacks against Las Vegas and now has 4.5, nine QB hits, 11 pressures and six tackles for loss. Gabe Jacas has 1.5 sacks and an interception, and five others have one sack each, among them Christian Elliss and Christian Barmore. Run defense is still 30th in EPA per rush.

The pass defense ranks 8th in EPA per dropback. Christian Gonzalez has allowed 8 catches for 43 yards on 18 targets (51.6 rating) with five passes defensed. Marcus Jones has an interception but has allowed 239 yards and two touchdowns on 27 targets (100.7). Craig Woodson is at 79.2, while Kevin Byard (127.1) and Charles Woods (153 yards on 18 targets) have been picked on most.

New England allows a 93.2 passer rating in coverage (18th; league 92.4) and 7.4 yards per target (13th). The cornerbacks are 9th best among cornerback groups at 88.0 on 88 targets. Safeties have improved again to 104.4 (19th), and linebackers are at 106.2 (25th), with Christian Elliss allowing 18 of 24 for 205 yards.

Andy Borregales is 6 of 8 on field goals with a long of 50 and 12 for 12 on extra points. Mitch Wishnowsky averages 47.3 yards gross and 39.6 net on 16 punts, seven inside the 20. Kyle Williams averages 24.6 yards on 14 kick returns and Marcus Jones 9.8 on nine punt returns. Special teams rank 23rd in DVOA.

The defense finally held up and the offense disappeared. In a 23–13 home loss to Minnesota, New Orleans allowed −0.10 EPA per play, its best defensive game of the season, but gained 142 yards at −0.35 EPA per play with three giveaways. At 1–4 and −33 in point differential, the offense has dropped to 23rd in EPA per play (from 15th) and the defense has edged up to 27th (from 30th), still 31st against the run and in success rate allowed. Giveaways (11) more than double takeaways (5).
DVOA has New Orleans 30th overall for a second week. The offense fell to 25th (from 21st), the defense is 31st and special teams dropped to 26th (from 19th).

A spread offense with 2.6 receivers per snap (6th most) and few tight ends (23rd). Defenses show it light boxes on 65% of runs, the most in the league (league 45%), and New Orleans hasn't taken advantage (−0.12 EPA per run, 23rd). The defense keeps more linemen on the field than any team and the fewest linebackers. Blitzing has stopped backfiring: sending five or more is now at +0.10 EPA per dropback against +0.20 with four rushers (league −0.01 and +0.10).

Motion helps the passing game a little and the run game not at all. New Orleans motions on 58% of plays (16th; league 58%); dropbacks with motion are at +0.02 EPA against −0.10 without, while runs after motion fall to −0.16 against −0.03 without. The defense is hurt badly by it: runs after motion gain 5.6 yards with a 57% success rate and +0.22 EPA, all last in the league, compared with −0.26 EPA (6th) when the offense stays still.

Tyler Shough had his worst game against Minnesota, 16 of 25 for 96 yards and 2 interceptions (38.1 passer rating), and is now 25th of 37 qualifiers at −0.03 EPA per dropback. His accuracy is still above average (completions 2.5 points over expectation, Next Gen Stats), with 9 touchdowns, 5 interceptions and an 88.7 rating. The blitz is the biggest drag (−0.22 EPA per dropback when opponents send extra rushers, +0.06 when they don't). Play action works (+0.23 vs. −0.08) but New Orleans uses it on 16% of dropbacks, the fewest in the league.

Nobody has gotten the run game going. Travis Etienne leads with 128 yards at 4.3 per carry but is half a yard below Next Gen Stats' expectation (35th of 42 qualifiers), Kendre Miller has 83 yards on 29 carries (−0.27 EPA per carry) and Alvin Kamara 86 on 28 (3.1 per carry). The backs gain 2.0 yards before contact per carry (27th). New Orleans breaks 3.2 tackles per game (tied for 9th), led by Etienne (4) and tight end Juwan Johnson (3).

Chris Olave remains the focal point, with 28% of the targets and 46% of the air yards, and has turned that into 39 catches for 537 yards and +0.70 EPA per target. Juwan Johnson is the best efficiency target: 25 catches on 32 targets, 3 touchdowns, 3.9 yards of separation (11th of 118) and 1.2 yards after the catch above expectation. Devaughn Vele (25 catches, 252 yards, 2 touchdowns) gets little separation (2.1 yards, 112th), Noah Fant has 3 touchdowns on 9 catches, and Bryce Lance has caught 5 of 16 deep targets.

Pass protection is average: pressure on 22% of dropbacks (15th) and a 5.8% sack rate (16th). Four linemen (Fuaga, Edwards, McCoy and Ruiz) have played every snap, with Asim Richards (62%) and Kelvin Banks (37%) splitting left tackle, and the line has only 6 accepted penalties, 3rd fewest. Runs up the middle work (3.5 yards per carry, +0.15 EPA, 48% success on 46 carries); runs behind right tackle have one success in 12 tries.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. The blame has evened out. With Weeks 4 and 5 charted, Shough has turned 13 of 49 pressures into sacks (27%, right at the league rate), down from 34% through Week 3. Of the 13 sacks, FTN put 6 on a standard rush, 4 on blitzes, 2 on Shough and 1 on an extended play; Minnesota's one came on a four-man rush.

The run defense is 31st in EPA per rush allowed (+0.02), and the pass rush has faded: 6.8 pressures per game (tied for 26th, from 16th) and a 5.7% sack rate (18th). Chase Young has been the bright spot with 4 sacks, 6 QB hits, 3 tackles for loss and a forced fumble. Carl Granderson adds 2.5 sacks and 4 tackles for loss, and linebacker Kaden Elliss has 6 pressures and 5 QB hits as a blitzer.

26th in EPA per dropback allowed. Kool-Aid McKinstry has played every snap with 4 passes defensed and a 98 passer rating allowed on 25 targets. The touchdowns have come at the other corner spot and safety: Quincy Riley has allowed 4 on 25 targets (120 rating) and Julian Blackmon 3 on 12, though Blackmon also has the unit's interception. Justin Reid has 6 missed tackles and a 112 rating allowed.

Coverage is near the bottom of the league: a 108.1 passer rating allowed (29th; league 92.4), 67% completions (28th) and 10 touchdowns against 1 interception. The corners have allowed a 119.1 rating (30th) and 5 touchdowns on 54 targets, and the safeties a 114.9 rating and 5 touchdowns while drawing 35% of the targets (league 23%). The linebackers have held up at 93.8 on 44 targets with no touchdowns.

Below average (26th in special teams DVOA, from 19th). Daniel Carlson is 5 of 7 on field goals with a long of 51 and 11 of 13 on extra points. Ryan Wright nets 40.8 yards per punt with 6 of 18 inside the 20, and Barion Brown averages 25.1 yards on 13 kickoff returns.

New York is 3–1–1 after a 27–27 overtime tie in Washington, with a +3 point differential. The roles flipped in Week 5: the offense had its best game since Week 1 (+0.07 EPA per play, 409 yards) and has climbed from 22nd to 17th in EPA per play, while the defense forced no takeaways and slipped from 17th to 22nd. It still allows only 21.2 points per game (9th), and the eight takeaways (seven giveaways) are among the most in the league.

DVOA still sees a below-average team and has dropped New York from 23rd to 27th overall. The offense is 29th, the defense has fallen from 17th to 23rd, and special teams (3rd) continue to do a lot of the work.

The Giants are still one of the most run-leaning offenses, 9.8 points below expected pass rate (31st), with two or more backs on 29% of snaps (league 20%) and 1.4 backs on the field on average (league 1.1). The heavy looks still don't produce: −0.09 EPA per play with two or more backs and +0.00 with one. On defense the blitz keeps paying off. FTN has them blitzing on 40% of dropbacks (4th), and five or more rushers hold passers to −0.16 EPA per dropback, while the four-man rush allows +0.20.

The Giants motion on only 48% of snaps (31st; league 58%), but the offense is better when they do: +0.05 EPA per play with motion (15th) against −0.08 without (23rd), the 8th-largest gain in the league. Passes after motion average +0.20 EPA against +0.05 without, and runs −0.08 against −0.37. The defense faces motion on 57% of snaps and handles it well (−0.03 EPA per play, 14th) but gives up +0.11 without it (27th).

Jameis Winston is up to −0.01 EPA per dropback (24th of 37 qualified), with six touchdowns, three interceptions and completions 3.9 points below expectation (35th). Week 5 was his best and busiest game: 33 of 54 for 326 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. The blitz is still the problem (−0.19 EPA per dropback vs. +0.24 without), and play action no longer helps (+0.03 vs. +0.12 without). Jaxson Dart's 38 dropbacks are still at +0.55.

Cam Skattebo has 81 carries at 3.6 yards per carry, 0.5 yards below Next Gen Stats' expectation (36th of 42 qualified) and −0.17 EPA per carry. The blocking doesn't help: 2.0 yards before contact per carry (26th; league 2.5), and Skattebo gets more after contact (2.0) than before it (1.6). Najee Harris has 27 carries at 3.6 yards each and −0.35 EPA per carry. Skattebo leads with four broken tackles, and the team has nine, 24th per game (Pro Football Reference charting).

Isaiah Likely is the top target with 48 (29% of the team's), 33 catches, 284 yards and four touchdowns at +0.33 EPA per target, 9th of the 15 receivers with 40 or more targets. Malik Nabers has 29 catches on 46 targets for 329 yards and two touchdowns (+0.20 EPA per target) and takes 35% of the air yards, but he is 1.0 yard below expected after the catch. Malachi Fields is the deep option (15.5-yard depth of target) with 146 yards on 17 targets, and Darnell Mooney has cooled to +0.10 EPA per target.

Andrew Thomas, Jon Runyan Jr. and Francis Mauigoa have played every snap, Jermaine Eluemunor 87%, and John Michael Schmitz and Bryan Hudson have split center. Pressure is better than average (21.0%, 10th), but the sack rate is 7.0% (24th), and the line has 13 accepted penalties (21st), five by Runyan, four of them false starts. Runs around left end work (6.6 yards per carry, +0.23 EPA), while the most-used lane, up the middle, averages 2.6 yards and −0.38 EPA.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Winston has turned 11 of his 33 pressures into sacks (33% vs. a 27% league rate, 30th of 40 qualified), but that rate is coming down from 41%. FTN has charged six of the team's 13 sacks to him, none in Week 5, when Washington's two came on a blitz and a rush won. The other seven are split: three rushes won, three blitzes and one extended play.

The pass rush finally showed up in Week 5 with five sacks of Jayden Daniels, lifting the season total to eight and the sack rate from last to 26th (4.4%). Pressure is still scarce at 6.2 credits per game (30th; league 9.4). Abdul Carter leads with seven pressures, six QB hits and two sacks, Tremaine Edmunds and cornerback Andru Phillips have two sacks each, and Brian Burns has five pressures while playing 38% of snaps. The run defense is 27th in EPA per rush.

Jevon Holland is still the playmaker, with three interceptions, four passes defensed, two forced fumbles and a 54.8 rating allowed. Greg Newsome II (16 of 28, 63.5 rating, an interception) and Andru Phillips (10 of 17, 66.8) have been the best corners. Deonte Banks has an interception and seven passes defensed but has allowed three touchdowns, as has Colton Hood (10 of 13, 138.5 rating). Linebackers Edmunds and Arvell Reese have each allowed 16 of 17, though Reese has an interception.

The coverage numbers held up reasonably well against Washington. New York is 12th in passer rating allowed (87.6, from 8th), 8th in yards per target (6.7) and 3rd in interceptions with six, although opponents complete 65.2% (26th). The safeties are the strength: a 55.2 rating on 38 targets with three interceptions, against a league 94.9. Cornerbacks are at 90.4 on 82 targets with six touchdowns allowed, and linebackers have allowed 34 of 37.

New York ranks 3rd in special teams DVOA. Dominic Zvada is 11 of 14 on field goals with a long of 56 after a 9-for-9 start, and 8 for 8 on extra points. Jordan Stout has put 11 of 18 punts inside the 20 with a 45.6-yard net, and Tyrone Tracy Jr. averages 32.4 yards on five kickoff returns.

New York is 2–3 after a 17–12 home win over Cleveland, its best defensive game: 198 yards allowed at −0.30 EPA per play. That lifted the defense from 15th to 5th in EPA per play, with the run defense 7th and points allowed tied for 5th (19.2 per game). The offense has gone the other way, from 12th to 19th, after 278 yards and −0.18 EPA per play. Takeaways (6) still outnumber giveaways (3).
DVOA has New York 22nd overall, up from 25th. The offense fell to 23rd, the defense rose to 17th, and special teams improved from 23rd to 16th.

New York lives in one-back sets (85% of snaps, league 74%), and the few two-back looks lose −0.33 EPA per play. The defense plays more defensive linemen than almost anyone (4.3 on average, 3rd) and fewer linebackers (28th). Both rush plans now hold up: four rushers allow about zero EPA per dropback (league +0.10) and five or more −0.04.

The Jets motion less than any team: 46% of snaps (32nd; league 58%) and 39% of passes (31st). Plays without motion have been better (+0.05 EPA vs. −0.11), and passes after motion average 4.1 yards, last in the league. On defense, the split flipped this week: plays without motion are held to −0.15 EPA (4th), while plays with motion gain +0.01 (20th).

Geno Smith still has no interceptions and six touchdowns, and his completions are 6.3 points over Next Gen Stats' expectation, now 4th after leading the league. Against Cleveland he went 17 of 30 for 182 yards, 9.4 points below expectation, on a 5.0-yard average depth of target. He ranks 22nd of 37 in EPA per dropback (+0.04), down from 14th, and his 6.9-yard depth of target is 32nd. Play action is no longer a big lever (+0.06 with it, +0.03 without).

Braelon Allen has taken the lead: 236 yards on 57 carries (4.1 per carry), 0.7 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (10th of 42), with six broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference charting). Breece Hall averages 3.2 on 51 carries, 0.2 below expectation (24th), with five broken tackles, and is still 10 for 10 as a receiver for 102 yards. New York ranks 6th in broken tackles per game but 25th in yards before contact (2.1 per carry).

Garrett Wilson gets 30% of targets and 43% of air yards: 31 catches, 374 yards, three touchdowns, +0.47 EPA per target. Kenyon Sadiq's 4.6 yards of separation rank 3rd of 118 NGS-qualified receivers. Adonai Mitchell is the deep threat on a 15.8-yard average depth of target, and Isaiah Williams has 151 yards on 14 targets. Drops are a problem: FTN charts 11, tied for 2nd most (league average 6.3).

Olu Fashanu, Josh Myers and Joe Tippmann have played every snap and Armand Membou all but one; Dylan Parham (179 snaps) and Jordan Meredith (130) share the fifth spot. Pressure comes on 23% of dropbacks (18th), but the 9.4% sack rate ranks 30th. Run blocking is still weak at 2.1 yards before contact per carry (25th), and runs up the middle average 2.8 yards. Accepted penalties rose from four to nine, with Tippmann at three.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Smith turns 40% of pressures into sacks (tied for 4th highest of 40; league 27%), yet FTN has charged none of his 16 sacks to him. Nine came against a standard rush, five on blitzes and two on extended plays; Cleveland's four split two standard rushes, a blitz and an extended play.

The rush broke out against Cleveland, and New York's sack rate now ranks 2nd (17 sacks). David Bailey has five sacks, 11 pressures, seven QB hits and six tackles for loss. Demario Davis, Jowon Briggs, Will McDonald and Kingsley Enagbare have two sacks each. Pressure volume is average (9.4 per game, 16th), and the run defense ranks 7th in EPA per rush.

The pass defense is 14th in EPA per dropback. Brandon Stephens has allowed 13 catches on 31 targets (72.1 rating), Azareye'h Thomas two touchdowns (101.3), Jarvis Brownlee two (110.0), and linebacker Jamien Sherwood 184 yards on 22 targets. Opponents have made only three interception-worthy throws (league average 4.9). Penalties are a cost: the secondary has 11 accepted for 153 yards, and New York gives up the most first downs by penalty (3.4 per game).

The Jets allow an 88.2 passer rating in coverage (13th; league 92.4) and 6.5 yards per target (4th). Minkah Fitzpatrick's is still the only interception in coverage, tied for 2nd fewest. Safeties are the best group at 66.5 (8th) and haven't allowed a touchdown. Cornerbacks (92.3, 14th) have allowed five of the six touchdowns, and linebackers sit at 103.2 (24th).

Special teams rank 16th in DVOA, up from 23rd. Jason Sanders is 8 of 9 on field goals with a long of 54 and 7 of 8 on extra points. Austin McNamara has punted 25 times at 47.0 yards gross and 40.3 net, nine inside the 20. Isaiah Williams averages 25.2 yards per kick return and 10.9 per punt return.

Philadelphia is 2–3 and has been outscored by 20 after a 19–17 loss at Jacksonville in which it gained 232 yards and averaged −0.61 EPA per rush. The offense is 30th in EPA per play and 31st in success rate, scoring 18.4 points per game (29th). The defense has been steadier, up from 27th to 24th in EPA per play and 14th in points allowed (22.4). The Eagles didn't turn it over in Week 5 and have five giveaways to three takeaways.
DVOA has the Eagles 23rd overall. The offense has dropped from 20th to 26th, the defense has risen from 22nd to 19th, and special teams are 7th.

The Eagles are still run-leaning (5.8 points below expected pass rate, 23rd), mostly out of three-receiver, one-back sets: one back on 82% of snaps (league 74%), at −0.10 EPA per play. The rare two-back looks have been worse (−0.39). On defense they rush four on 73% of dropbacks and blitz only 23% of the time (27th; league 31%), and that's still the right call: the four-man rush allows +0.04 EPA per dropback (league +0.10), while five or more have allowed +0.36.

Philadelphia motions on 57% of snaps (18th) and is below average either way: −0.10 EPA per play with motion (27th) and −0.16 without (28th). Motion still helps the passing game, −0.01 EPA per dropback after motion against −0.17 without, but runs after motion have been worse (−0.24 vs. −0.14). The defense is the reverse of the offense: −0.01 EPA per play allowed against motion (15th) but +0.20 without (31st).

Jalen Hurts is at −0.05 EPA per dropback (26th of 37 qualified), with eight touchdowns, three interceptions and completions 2.4 points below expectation. In Week 5 he played faster and riskier, going 21 of 40 for 220 yards and a touchdown with a 2.53-second average time to throw and 30% of throws into tight windows, both far from his norms (3.04 seconds, 7th longest; 14.3% tight-window rate). Play action has backfired all season (−0.30 EPA per dropback on 35 plays vs. −0.03 without), and so has the blitz (−0.21 vs. −0.00).

Saquon Barkley is still the best runner here at 5.1 yards per carry and 1.1 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (6th of 42 qualified), but his carries (36) and snaps are unchanged from a week ago, so he didn't play in Week 5 (inferred from the snap counts). Without him the run game collapsed: Will Shipley is at 2.9 yards per carry on 20 carries and Dameon Pierce has 14 yards on 11. Philadelphia has six broken tackles in five games, 31st per game (Pro Football Reference charting).

Dontayvion Wicks has become the lead receiver: 17 catches on 28 targets for 260 yards, +0.51 EPA per target, a 13.2-yard depth of target, 1.0 yard of YAC over expected per catch and 32% of the air yards. DeVonta Smith has 235 yards on 27 targets but only +0.05 EPA per target. Makai Lemon has 15 catches on 22 targets for 108 yards and works short (5.5-yard depth of target). Darius Cooper (four touchdowns on seven catches) and Dallas Goedert (two on 11, +0.45 EPA per target) have been the scorers, and FTN charts only two drops, tied for the fewest in the league.

Jordan Mailata has played every snap and Tyler Steen 95%, but Lane Johnson, Cam Jurgens and Drew Kendall didn't play in Week 5 (their snap totals didn't change), so Markel Bell took over at tackle and Willie Lampkin and Jake Majors filled the interior. Pressure (26.8%, 28th) and sacks (7.2%, 25th) are both below average, and Jurgens has four of the line's 13 accepted penalties. The most-used lane outside the middle, right tackle, averages 2.4 yards and −0.26 EPA per carry.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Hurts's quicker Week 5 changed the picture: he took one sack on 15 pressures, and his pressure-to-sack rate is down to 27%, right at the 27% league rate (36% a week ago). FTN charged that sack to him, seven of his 13 in all. The other six were four rushes won, one blitz and one extended play.

Jalen Carter now leads the front with eight pressures, three sacks, five tackles for loss and three forced fumbles. Jalyx Hunt has seven pressures and four QB hits, Moro Ojomo six pressures, and Nolan Smith two sacks. As a group the rush is still thin: 7.6 pressure credits per game (23rd; league 9.4) and six sacks, a 3.1% sack rate that ranks 30th. The run defense ranks 26th in EPA per rush, despite five tackles for loss from Zack Baun.

Philadelphia is 24th in pass defense EPA. Quinyon Mitchell has been the best corner (17 of 28, a 64.3 rating) and added an interception. Cooper DeJean has allowed two touchdowns from the slot but has an interception and four passes defensed, and Andrew Mukuba has an interception but has allowed 166 yards on nine targets. Riq Woolen has allowed 209 yards and two touchdowns on 26 targets (109.3 rating).

Philadelphia is 16th in coverage passer rating (90.9) and has allowed six touchdowns, 6th fewest, with three interceptions. Linebackers (83.9 rating on 56 targets) and cornerbacks (85.0 on 97, against a league 93.0) have both held up. The safeties are the hole: 13 of 16 for 275 yards, 17.2 yards per target and a 132.3 rating.

Philadelphia ranks 7th in special teams DVOA. Jake Elliott is 5 for 5 on field goals with a long of 58 and 11 for 11 on extra points. Braden Mann has put 12 of 25 punts inside the 20 with a 43.8-yard net, and Britain Covey averages 12.6 yards per punt return.

3–2 after a 34–22 win over Indianapolis, Pittsburgh's best offensive game of the season (+0.24 EPA per play, +0.43 per run). The offense has now been positive three weeks running and has climbed from 28th to 21st in EPA per play, with the run game 4th. The defense has gone the other way: 18th in EPA per play (from 14th), and it has allowed positive EPA in three straight games, though only barely against the Colts.
DVOA moved Pittsburgh from 21st to 14th (4.8%). The offense climbed from 18th to 12th (3.9%), the defense holds at 13th (−3.8%), and special teams are 25th.

Pittsburgh passes more than its situations would predict (7 points over expected, 5th highest). One-back sets, used on 80% of snaps, are still the problem at −0.17 EPA per play, while two-back looks (+0.40, best in the league) and empty sets (+0.53) have worked in smaller doses. On defense, the four-man rush (−0.06 EPA per dropback) has been far better than sending five or more (+0.35, 28th). Pittsburgh has the 2nd most linebackers on the field (4.1 on average).

Pittsburgh motions less than almost anyone (49% of snaps, 29th; league 58%), and motion makes little difference to the offense now: pass plays average −0.10 EPA either way, and runs gain +0.02 EPA and 5.4 yards with motion against +0.11 and 4.5 without. The defense faces motion on 64% of plays (7th most) and has handled it (−0.04 EPA per play vs. +0.07 without), especially on runs (3.3 yards per carry vs. 5.3).

Aaron Rodgers is 28th of 37 qualified quarterbacks in EPA per dropback (−0.08), with 10 touchdowns and four interceptions, and completions remain below expectation (−2.0 points by NGS). Week 5 was his cleanest game: 22 of 31 for 235 yards and three touchdowns, almost all of it short (4.1-yard average depth, 5.0 yards short of the sticks). Play action is still the whole story: +0.40 EPA per dropback with it and −0.22 without, now the widest gap in the league, and blitzes hurt (−0.38 vs. −0.01). His receivers have nine drops, tied for 5th most.

Jaylen Warren is one of the league's best runners by Next Gen Stats: 5.9 yards per carry and 1.9 yards per carry over expectation, 2nd of 42 qualified backs, with +0.09 EPA per carry. His 12 broken tackles (seven on runs, five after catches) are tied for 2nd in the league (Pro Football Reference charting), and 225 of his 410 rushing yards came after contact. Pittsburgh ranks 3rd in broken tackles per game (4.2). Rico Dowdle is still at 2.5 yards per carry and a 13% success rate on 15 carries.

DK Metcalf leads with 37 targets (21%) and 35% of the air yards but has 19 catches for 225 yards, slightly below break-even per target (−0.03 EPA), with three drops and 2.2 yards of separation (107th of 118 NGS-tracked receivers). Roman Wilson remains the downfield option (14.5-yard depth, two touchdowns, +0.25 EPA per target), and Pat Freiermuth has four touchdowns on 26 targets. Tight end Darnell Washington leads all 118 tracked receivers in YAC over expectation (4.6 per catch), and Warren has added 230 receiving yards on 26 targets.

Zach Frazier and Mason McCormick have played every snap and Troy Fautanu all but one, while Max Iheanachor and Brock Hoffman (60% each) have taken more of the other two spots from Dylan Cook and Spencer Anderson (40% each). Pressure arrives on 22% of dropbacks (13th lowest) and the sack rate is 6.9% (21st), with only one sack against Indianapolis. Run blocking is 21st in yards before contact (2.2 per carry), but runs off left guard have averaged 7.9 yards. The line has drawn seven accepted penalties, tied for 4th fewest.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Week 4's spike didn't carry over: after FTN charged all five sacks at Cleveland to Rodgers, he was sacked once against Indianapolis, on a blitz. Six of his 14 sacks are on the quarterback, and he turns 33% of pressures into sacks (tied for 12th highest of 40; league 27%). Of the rest, four came against blitzes, two on extended plays and two on a standard rush.

T.J. Watt has 4.5 sacks, eight pressures, seven QB hits, six tackles for loss and an interception. Alex Highsmith has three sacks and five tackles for loss, Cameron Heyward six pressures and four passes defensed, and Payton Wilson six tackles for loss. Pressure volume is low (6.4 per game, 28th; league 9.4), and the sack rate has slipped from 8th to 14th. The run defense is 18th in EPA per rush.

Pass defense has slipped to 19th in EPA per dropback (from 16th). Patrick Queen (a 50 passer rating on 23 targets, an interception) and Jaquan Brisker (60, an interception) lead a strong second level. The corners are still the leak: Jalen Ramsey has allowed three touchdowns (a 116 rating), Asante Samuel Jr. 278 yards on 30 targets despite seven passes defensed, and Daylen Everette 186 yards on 19 targets.

Pittsburgh allows the lowest completion rate in the league (54%) and an 80.0 passer rating (7th; league 92.4), though 7.5 yards per target ranks 14th. Corners have allowed a 103.5 rating and all six touchdowns on 92 targets (league 93.0 for corners), while safeties (49.9) and linebackers (70.5) are far better than the league marks (94.9 and 91.3). Four interceptions in coverage are tied for 8th.

Chris Boswell is 9 of 12 on field goals with a long of 56. Cameron Johnston nets 43.9 yards per punt with 10 of 21 inside the 20, and Kaden Wetjen averages 22.5 yards on 19 kick returns. Special teams rank 25th in DVOA, but Pittsburgh has only two special teams penalties, tied for 2nd fewest.

A top-two defense carrying an offense that is getting worse. Seattle is 3–2 at +29, 2nd in defensive EPA per play and success rate, 2nd against the pass and 3rd against the run. The offense has fallen to 24th in EPA per play (13th a week ago): 16th through the air and 30th on the ground. The 32–29 loss to San Francisco was its worst game yet, −0.43 EPA per play with 4 giveaways, even though the defense held the 49ers to −0.14 and took the ball away 3 times.
DVOA has Seattle 8th (16.4%) with the No. 2 defense (−23.2%). The offense is 22nd and special teams 8th.

Seattle plays two or more backs on 26% of plays (league 20%) and uses play action on 33% of dropbacks, 2nd most, where it gains +0.32 EPA per dropback against −0.03 without. The defense plays the 4th-fewest defensive linemen and 5th-most defensive backs, blitzes on 21% of dropbacks (4th lowest) and rushes four on 76%, holding offenses to −0.05 EPA per dropback when it does (league +0.10).

Seattle uses motion on 58% of plays (17th) and is worse with it: −0.14 EPA per play against +0.01 without. Runs after motion average −0.35 EPA, the worst in the league. The defense is the best in the league against motion (−0.20) and 8th without it (−0.06).

Sam Darnold has fallen to 31st of 37 qualifiers at −0.10 EPA per dropback, with 7 touchdowns and 5 interceptions. Against San Francisco he threw 2 interceptions, completed 1.7 points below expectation (his first negative game) and was sacked 5 times. He holds the ball 3.2 seconds per throw, 2nd longest among qualifiers. Drew Lock (+0.48 in Weeks 1–2) still leads all qualifiers. Opponents blitz Seattle on 38% of dropbacks (5th most), and the offense is about the same either way (+0.11 EPA per dropback against the blitz, +0.07 without).

The run game is 30th in EPA per carry (−0.27). Emanuel Wilson averages 3.4 yards per carry, −0.66 under Next Gen Stats' expectation (37th of 42), at −0.24 EPA per carry. Jadarian Price (4.3 per carry, −0.44 EPA) and George Holani (3.0, −0.46) haven't helped. The backs get 2.3 yards before contact (19th), and Seattle has 8 broken tackles (1.6 per game, tied for 28th).

Jaxon Smith-Njigba is still one of the most featured receivers in the league: 35% of the targets and half the air yards, turned into 37 catches, 583 yards, 7 touchdowns and +0.69 EPA per target. Cooper Kupp has caught 11 of 15 for 129 yards and a touchdown (+0.45). Rashid Shaheed (9 of 19, −0.44 EPA per target, the lowest yards after catch over expectation of 118 qualifiers) and AJ Barner (3 drops, −0.39) remain drags.

Pressure allowed is the problem: 30% of dropbacks, 2nd most in the league, and the sack rate is up to 6.8% (20th) after 5 sacks against the 49ers. Charles Cross, Abraham Lucas, Grey Zabel and Jalen Sundell have played every snap while Christian Haynes, Beau Stephens and Anthony Bradford share right guard. Runs up the middle (2.9 yards per carry, −0.41 EPA on 37 carries) and behind left guard (−0.57 on 15) are the worst lanes.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. The answer is increasingly Darnold: FTN charged all 5 sacks against San Francisco to him, so 8 of Seattle's 11 sacks are his fault, with 2 on extended plays and 1 when a standard rush won. He is pressured on 35% of dropbacks, 2nd most among qualifiers, and turns 23% of pressures into sacks (league 27%).

A top-three run defense (−0.21 EPA per rush) with a rush that gets home: 11.8 pressures per game (6th) and 14 sacks (7.6% rate, 8th). Leonard Williams has 3 sacks, 11 pressures, 7 QB hits and 5 tackles for loss, and Byron Murphy 3 sacks and 5 tackles for loss. Derick Hall has 2 sacks and 7 QB hits, DeMarcus Lawrence 9 pressures, and Ernest Jones 50 tackles, 2 sacks and an interception.

2nd against the pass, with takeaways throughout. Julian Love has 2 interceptions and a 14 passer rating allowed, Nehemiah Pritchett 2 interceptions and a 32 rating, and Devon Witherspoon has allowed 118 yards and no touchdowns on 27 targets. Josh Jobe (2 touchdowns, 106 rating, 1 interception) is the one starter opponents have beaten.

Among the best coverage numbers in the league by PFR charting: a 70.2 passer rating allowed (2nd; league 92.4), 5.4 yards per target (2nd) and 7 interceptions (tied with Green Bay for most). Opponents are 96 of 162 for 867 yards and 7 touchdowns. Linebackers see 33% of the targets (2nd most; league 27%) and allow a 67.1 rating, and all three groups rank in the top seven. Ernest Jones is the most targeted defender (31 targets, 58.7 rating).

8th in special teams DVOA. Jason Myers is 10 for 10 on field goals with a long of 57 and 14 of 15 on extra points. Michael Dickson nets 42.8 yards per punt with 8 of 20 inside the 20, and Rashid Shaheed averages 27.6 yards per kickoff return.

Still unbeaten and still the best team by DVOA: 5–0 with a +61 point differential, the best in the league. San Francisco is 2nd in offensive EPA per play (+0.21, behind Buffalo), 1st in success rate and 1st in passing EPA, and the defense has climbed to 4th (16th a week ago). Week 5 was won the other way: the offense posted its first negative game (−0.14 EPA per play, 3 giveaways) in a 32–29 win at Seattle, and the defense held the Seahawks to −0.43 with 4 takeaways.
DVOA has San Francisco 1st at 52.2%, with the No. 1 offense (36.4%) and No. 4 defense (−18.6%). Special teams rank 24th.

Still the most creative usage in the league. San Francisco has the 3rd-most backs on the field (1.4 per snap, with Kyle Juszczyk at fullback) and plays with two or more backs on 32% of plays (league 20%). It goes empty on 14% (league 6%) and averages +0.76 EPA per play there on 38 snaps. On defense, sending five or more (−0.16 EPA per dropback) has been far better than four (+0.09).

San Francisco uses motion on 79% of plays, the most in the league, and is elite either way: +0.17 EPA per play with motion (2nd) and +0.34 without (1st). The defense is 3rd best against motion (−0.13) but 17th without it (+0.02).

Brock Purdy is 2nd of 37 qualifiers at +0.41 EPA per dropback (only Drew Lock, on 51 dropbacks, is higher), with 13 touchdowns, 2 interceptions and a 119.3 passer rating. Seattle sacked him for the first time this season, three times, and he threw his second interception, but he still completed 10.5 points above expectation that day. FTN has charted 4 interception-worthy throws for the offense (league average 4.9). Blitzing him still backfires: +0.70 EPA per dropback against the blitz, +0.30 without.

Christian McCaffrey is efficient rather than dominant: 286 yards at 4.7 per carry, +0.35 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (14th of 42), +0.05 EPA per carry, plus 19 catches for 137 yards on 25 targets. He has 5 of the team's 10 broken tackles (2.0 per game, tied for 21st). Kaelon Black (3.7 per carry, −0.75 over expected, 39th of 42) is still a step down, and Deebo Samuel Sr. has 78 yards on 9 carries.

Production is spread across four players. Mike Evans leads in efficiency (+1.04 EPA per target, 326 yards, 3 touchdowns, 43% of the air yards) despite 1.6 yards of separation, 2nd lowest of 118 qualifiers. George Kittle has 268 yards, 4 touchdowns and 2.1 yards after the catch above expectation (8th). Deebo Samuel Sr. has 16 catches for 206 yards and 3 touchdowns on short throws (3.0-yard average depth) with 4.7 yards of separation, 2nd most.

Still elite in pass protection: pressure on 18% of dropbacks (3rd lowest; league 23%) and a 1.9% sack rate, the lowest in the league, even after the first 3 sacks of the season at Seattle. Colton McKivitz and Connor Colby have played every snap, Dominick Puni and Jake Brendel nearly all of them, and Trent Williams 90%. The 2.9 yards before contact per carry ranks 7th, though Purdy's scrambles lift it (McCaffrey alone is at 2.8). Runs behind right guard (−0.15 EPA on 21 carries) and off left end (−0.17 on 13) are the weakest lanes.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Purdy's first three sacks all came at Seattle: FTN charged two to him, against a four-man and a five-man rush, and the third came on an extended play outside the pocket. He has turned 3 of 28 pressures into sacks (11%; league 27%), so the credit is still mostly his and the line's.

A pass rush with more volume than finish (10.8 pressures per game, 12th; 5.8% sack rate, 17th), but 5 of its 11 sacks came against Seattle. Keion White leads with 3 sacks, 9 pressures and 4 tackles for loss, and Osa Odighizuwa has 9 pressures and 6 QB hits. Fred Warner has 50 tackles and 3 forced fumbles, and Nick Bosa has 4 pressures in a part-time role. The run defense is now 5th in EPA per rush (−0.17).

13th against the pass, up from 18th. Renardo Green has 3 interceptions and a 45 passer rating allowed on 24 targets, and Marques Sigle has allowed 2 catches on 7 targets. Deommodore Lenoir (159 yards on 26 targets, 98 rating) has slipped. Upton Stout (253 yards on 26 targets, 116 rating) and Jack Jones (2 touchdowns, 115 rating in a part-time role) remain the weak spots.

Better in coverage than the EPA rank suggests. San Francisco allows an 84.9 passer rating (11th; league 92.4) and 6.3 yards per target (3rd), with 6 touchdowns (tied for 6th fewest) and 3 interceptions. Cornerbacks draw 52% of the targets (8th most; league 46%) at an 89.4 rating. The safeties are barely tested (17% of targets, 3rd lowest) and allow a 48.3 rating, the best of any safety group.

Below average (24th in special teams DVOA). Eddy Pineiro is 5 of 8 on field goals with a long of 57 and 17 of 19 on extra points. Corliss Waitman nets 43.6 yards per punt with 9 of 16 inside the 20, and Deebo Samuel Sr. averages 25.5 yards per kickoff return.

The first win arrived on Thursday night, 24–16 at Dallas, and it was the offense's best game: +0.16 EPA per play, 421 yards and no giveaways, while the defense added three takeaways. At 1–4, Tampa Bay has climbed to 27th in offensive EPA per play (from 31st) and 29th passing (from 32nd), and its 9.0% sack rate is no longer the league's worst (29th).
