The defense is 8th in EPA per play and 4th against the run, and all four losses were by seven points or fewer. Giveaways (9) now barely outnumber takeaways (7).

DVOA has Tampa Bay 12th overall (from 18th), far kinder than the record; only Houston (11th) rates higher among 1–4 teams. The defense is up to 5th (from 9th), the offense to 18th (from 24th) and special teams to 9th (from 14th).

The offense lives in three-receiver sets, with 2.7 wideouts per snap (3rd most) and few tight ends (25th). The defense is one of the most aggressive in the league, blitzing on 41% of dropbacks by FTN's count (3rd), and that remains its best weapon: −0.28 EPA per dropback when sending five or more (4th), against +0.23 with four rushers (28th). It also loads the box against the run, with eight or more on 22% of runs, the most in the league (league 9%).

No offense depends on motion more. Tampa Bay motions on 73% of plays (3rd; league 58%) and is break-even with it (+0.01 EPA per play) but collapses without it (−0.36, last in the league), the biggest motion gain anywhere at +0.37. The split is starkest on dropbacks: 0.00 EPA and 6.2 yards per play with motion, −0.43 and 3.5 yards without. Runs come after motion 83% of the time, the highest rate in the league. On defense, the run stops are best when the offense stays still (−0.27 EPA per carry, 5th).

Jalon Daniels has started the last two games and was sharp at Dallas: 19 of 25 for 189 yards, a touchdown and no interceptions (110.3 passer rating), almost all on short throws (4.1-yard average intended air yards). For the season he is at +0.05 EPA per dropback on 71 dropbacks (20th of 37 qualifiers) with completions 1.7 points above expectation (Next Gen Stats), 2 touchdowns and 3 interceptions. Baker Mayfield remains last among qualifiers at −0.26 EPA per dropback. Play action still hasn't helped (−0.37 EPA per dropback against −0.06 without, 31st).

Bucky Irving broke out at Dallas: with that game charted by Pro Football Reference, his broken tackles jumped from 2 to 12 (10 on runs), tied for 2nd in the league. For the season he is at 5.3 yards per carry (6th of 42 qualifiers), 1.1 over Next Gen Stats' expectation (7th) and +0.08 EPA per carry. That one game moved Tampa Bay from 28th to 5th in broken tackles per game (3.6). The backs gain 2.8 yards before contact per carry (10th). Irving has 15 catches for 71 yards and a touchdown, and Kenny Gainwell has 44 yards on 17 carries.

Chris Godwin Jr. is the most efficient target, catching 19 of 21 for 179 yards and +0.33 EPA per target with 4.0 yards of separation (9th of 118). Emeka Egbuka leads with 33 targets (21 catches, 192 yards) but is at −0.04 EPA per target, and Cade Otton (18 catches, 182 yards) has 3 of the team's 7 FTN-charted drops (league average 6.3). Ted Hurst III runs the deepest routes (17.8-yard average depth of target, 2nd) with 1.8 yards of separation and has caught 8 of 16 for a touchdown. Tez Johnson has 138 yards on 10 targets.

The five starters (Wirfs, Goedeke, Barton, Mauch and Bredeson) have played nearly every snap (Wirfs and Mauch have missed one each). Pressure allowed is middling (24.5%, 21st), which suggests the 29th-ranked sack rate is mostly about what happens after the pressure; see Who owns the sacks. Penalties are a problem: 17 accepted flags on the line (31st), 10 of them holding, with Barton charged with 5. Backs gain 2.8 yards before contact per carry (10th), and runs outside the left tackle (8.4 yards per carry) and left end (7.4) work, while runs up the middle average 2.1.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, a measure that mostly reflects the QB) plus FTN's charting of each sack. It points at Mayfield more than the line. Mayfield turns pressure into sacks at 45% (3rd highest of 40; league 27%), while Daniels is at 24% (4 of 17). Of the 17 sacks, FTN charged 5 to the quarterback, 5 came on extended plays outside the pocket and 6 on blitzes, including 3 of Daniels' 4; only one came on a standard rush with no blitz.

A strong run defense (4th in EPA per rush) and a pass rush that depends on the blitz: 7.2 pressures per game (25th) and a 3.4% sack rate (28th). Linebacker David Walker has 2 sacks and 3 tackles for loss in 71 snaps, Josiah Trotter has an interception, a sack, 3 tackles for loss and 39 tackles, and A'Shawn Robinson has a sack and an interception. Alex Anzalone has struggled in coverage, allowing 20 catches on 28 targets for 286 yards and a 113 passer rating.

17th against the pass. Jacob Parrish has 7 passes defensed and an interception with an 84 passer rating allowed on 28 targets, Zyon McCollum has 6 passes defensed (99 rating) and Benjamin Morrison is at 78 on 17 targets. Tykee Smith has allowed 3 touchdowns and a 111 rating on 22 targets, and Keionte Scott has allowed 16 catches on 20 targets with 7 missed tackles.

A 92.5 passer rating allowed (17th; league 92.4) and 7.6 yards per target (20th), with opponents completing 64% of charted targets (22nd). The 5 interceptions are tied for 6th, and opponents have dropped 13 passes by FTN's count, the most in the league. The linebackers are at 82.5 with 3 interceptions despite Anzalone, the corners at 97.8 on 88 targets and the safeties at 108.3.

Up to 9th in special teams DVOA. Chase McLaughlin is 10 for 10 on field goals with a long of 59 and 10 for 10 on extra points. Kenny Gainwell (26.0) and Kameron Johnson (27.5) give Tampa Bay a strong kickoff return pair. Riley Dixon nets 37.1 yards per punt with only 5 of 21 inside the 20, the soft spot.

Tennessee is 0–5 after a 3–26 home loss to Houston, its worst game of the season: 187 yards, −0.39 EPA per play and two turnovers. The offense now scores a league-low 11.6 points per game and ranks 31st in EPA per play, and it still passes 9.1 points less often than expected (28th in PROE). The defense keeps games closer than the record suggests (21.8 points allowed per game, tied for 10th), but the point differential is now −51.
DVOA has Tennessee 31st overall (−39.0%), down from 29th, with the 27th-ranked offense, the 30th-ranked defense and the 29th-ranked special teams.

The Titans play more three-receiver sets than anyone (2.73 receivers per snap, 1st; league 2.43) and fewer tight ends (1.24, league 1.44). Their two-back looks keep getting worse (−0.40 EPA per play on 20% of snaps). Runs against light boxes are still positive (+0.08 EPA on 56% of runs), while seven-man boxes have cost −0.37 per run. On defense, sending five or more rushers keeps going badly (+0.62 EPA per dropback on 36 plays), while the four-man rush allows +0.12.

Tennessee uses presnap motion on 48% of plays (30th; league 58%), and its motion plays are the league's worst: −0.27 EPA per play with motion (32nd) against −0.04 without. The gap shows up on runs (−0.23 EPA per carry with motion, +0.14 without) and passes (−0.31 with, 32nd, vs. −0.10 without). On defense the run defense is about break-even against motion (28th) but strong without it (−0.22 EPA per run, 8th).

Cam Ward had a rough Week 5 against Houston: 23 of 36 for 170 yards, no touchdowns, an interception and 4 sacks. For the season he is at −0.19 EPA per dropback (35th of 37 qualifiers) with completions 1.1% below expectation by Next Gen Stats, 3 touchdowns and 3 interceptions. He is still among the most cautious passers in the league, throwing into tight windows on 8.4% of attempts (3rd lowest; league 15.3%), and his average throw lands 2.8 yards short of the sticks. Play action has hurt (−0.38 EPA per dropback with it, −0.13 without).

Tony Pollard is still beating Next Gen Stats' expectation (0.19 yards per carry, 17th of 42 qualifiers) at 4.0 yards per carry and −0.06 EPA per carry on 68 carries. Tyjae Spears has 65 yards on 17 carries and 14 catches for 68 yards, and leads the team with 4 broken tackles after the catch. Tennessee has 9 broken tackles in five games, 1.8 per game and tied for 24th in Pro Football Reference charting; Pollard has three on runs.

Rookie Carnell Tate is still the clear No. 1 with 37 targets (26% share) and 49% of the air yards, but his efficiency has faded: he is at 23 catches for 274 yards and +0.06 EPA per target, down from +0.16. Wan'Dale Robinson has been the more efficient option (22 of 30, two touchdowns, +0.29 EPA per target). Elic Ayomanor remains the big-play threat with 130 yards and a touchdown on 6 catches, while Gunnar Helm is at −0.19 EPA per target.

Pass protection slipped in Week 5: Houston sacked Ward 4 times, pressure is up to 25.2% of dropbacks (23rd) and the sack rate to 5.7% (15th). Four linemen have played every snap, while right guard rotates among Atonio Mafi (44%), Fernando Carmona (36%) and Jackson Slater (20%). Runs behind left tackle are still the problem (22 carries at 2.5 yards, −0.50 EPA each). JC Latham has 5 accepted penalties and Dan Moore Jr. drew all 3 of his against Houston.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Through Week 4 the sacks pointed at the quarterback, but Week 5 shifted the picture: FTN charted three of Houston's four as a standard rush beating the line and one as a blitz. Ward's 10 sacks are now 4 standard rushes, 3 his own fault, 2 extended plays and 1 blitz, and he still converts pressure to sacks below the league rate (22.7% vs. 26.6%).

The pass rush is thin as a unit: 6.2 pressures per game is tied for 30th and the 6.1% sack rate is 16th. Jacob Martin leads with 9 pressures and 2.5 sacks on 57% of snaps, Jeffery Simmons has 6 pressures, 2 sacks, 5 QB hits and 4 tackles for loss, and John Franklin-Myers adds 6 pressures and 1.5 sacks. The run defense is 17th in EPA per rush.

27th in pass defense EPA. Marcus Harris has allowed a 72.3 passer rating with an interception, and Amani Hooker has an interception but has allowed 180 yards on 17 targets. Alontae Taylor has allowed 18 catches on 21 targets for 159 yards (114.1 rating) and adds a sack and 4 tackles for loss, while Cordale Flott has given up 10 of 14 for 131.

The Titans still give up completions: opponents complete 74.1% of passes in coverage (31st), but have only 5 touchdowns (tied for 4th fewest) on 143 targets. The passer rating allowed is 103.5 (27th; league 92.4) at 8.1 yards per target. Linebackers see 32% of targets (league 27%) and have allowed a 111.3 rating, with Anthony Hill giving up 2 touchdowns on 23 targets.

The coverage units remain the issue. Tommy Townsend has punted 25 times at 48.9 gross but 41.5 net yards, with 8 inside the 20. Joey Slye is 5 of 6 on field goals with a long of 42, and Chimere Dike returns both kicks (25.8 yards on 19) and punts (7.1). DVOA ranks the unit 29th, and 9 accepted special-teams penalties are tied for 3rd most.

Washington is 1–3–1 after a 27–27 overtime tie with the Giants, and has been outscored by 34 while allowing 29.8 points per game (30th). Jayden Daniels's return lifted the offense from 21st to 15th in EPA per play (+0.10 per play in Week 5), though it is still 26th in success rate. The defense is 23rd, but it has seven takeaways in the last three games, and Washington's +5 turnover margin is tied for 2nd in the league.
DVOA is still harsh. Washington is 28th overall, with the 24th-ranked offense (up from 27th), 22nd-ranked defense and 30th-ranked special teams.

The offense lives in one-back sets (85% of snaps, league 74%), and those plays sit at −0.04 EPA. The defense blitzes on 46% of dropbacks, the 2nd-highest rate in the league (league 31%), and it's still better than the four-man rush, though the edge has narrowed: +0.07 EPA per dropback with five or more rushers vs. +0.16 with four.

Washington motions on 54% of snaps (22nd) and gets the 3rd-biggest lift in the league from it: +0.10 EPA per play with motion (9th) against −0.15 without (27th). Passes after motion average +0.18 EPA against −0.08 without, and runs after motion succeed 45% of the time against 31% without. On defense motion makes little difference (+0.03 EPA per play with it, +0.05 without).

Jayden Daniels returned in Week 5 and went 17 of 25 for 199 yards, with completions 5.1 points above expectation and a quick 2.41-second average time to throw. For the season he is at +0.19 EPA per dropback (12th of 37 qualified) with three touchdowns and no interceptions. Marcus Mariota (+0.09, four touchdowns, no interceptions) and Athan Kaliakmanis (−0.30 on 36 dropbacks) filled in from Week 2 to Week 4. The offense still struggles against the blitz (−0.20 EPA per dropback vs. +0.17 without).

Jacory Croskey-Merritt still has the most carries (67) at 3.6 yards per carry, 0.45 below Next Gen Stats' expectation (32nd of 42 qualified, up from 2nd-worst), and he has his first broken tackle on a run. Rachaad White has been more productive: 4.1 yards per carry on 29 carries and three broken tackles on runs (Pro Football Reference charting). The team's 3.4 yards before contact per carry (3rd) is lifted by Daniels's scrambles; Croskey-Merritt gets 2.2 and White 2.4, close to the 2.5 league average.

Stefon Diggs leads with 31 targets and three touchdowns on 18 catches, but only 5.5 yards per target, and he wasn't targeted in Week 5. Terry McLaurin (26 targets, 12.5-yard depth of target) has been the most efficient at +0.47 EPA per target. Antonio Williams has 15 catches on 22 targets (+0.23), while Dyami Brown runs the deepest routes (17.4-yard depth of target) at −0.27 EPA per target. Treylon Burks has two touchdowns on five catches.

Josh Conerly and Chris Paul have played every snap and Brandon Coleman 97%, while Nick Allegretti, Samuel Cosmi, Lucas Patrick and Matt Gulbin have rotated through the interior. Pressure is still a problem (26.0% of dropbacks, 26th), and the Giants' five sacks pushed the sack rate from 3.2% (2nd) to 5.2% (10th). The line has only seven accepted penalties (4th fewest), but the team has eight team-level penalties (four of them delay of game), the most in the league. The right side still struggles in the run game: right guard averages 2.0 yards and −0.31 EPA on 22 carries, and right tackle 2.7 yards and −0.34.

No public stat measures this directly, because the time of each sack isn't released. The best free combination is pressure-to-sack rate (how often pressure becomes a sack, mostly a QB measure) plus FTN's charting of each sack. Ten of 50 pressures have become sacks (20% vs. a 27% league rate). Daniels is at 6 of 22 (27%) and Mariota 3 of 21 (14%). Of Daniels's five sacks against the Giants, FTN charged only the one in overtime to him, the first on a Washington quarterback this season; three came on blitzes and one on an extended play.

The pass rush creates pressure, 11.4 pressure credits per game (7th; league 9.4), but has nine sacks (4.2%, 27th). K'Lavon Chaisson leads with 12 pressures, 2.5 sacks and seven QB hits, Odafe Oweh has eight pressures and two sacks, and Daron Payne has eight pressures from the interior. Sonny Styles has a sack, an interception, a forced fumble and three tackles for loss. The run defense has climbed from 13th to 6th in EPA per rush.

Still the weak spot. Mike Sainristil has allowed 13 of 18 for five touchdowns (a 144.7 rating), and safety Jeremy Reaves three touchdowns and 188 yards on 17 targets. Amik Robertson has eight passes defensed on 39 targets (an 88.4 rating), and Rasul Douglas has held opponents to a 59.7 rating with an interception.

Washington is 26th in passer rating allowed (103.5, up from 28th), and its 14 coverage touchdowns allowed rank 30th. Safeties (135.2 rating, five touchdowns on 35 targets) and cornerbacks (104.9, seven touchdowns) are both above the league averages of 94.9 and 93.0. The linebackers remain the exception at 74.2 on 60 targets, with interceptions from Sonny Styles and Kain Medrano.

Washington ranks 30th in special teams DVOA, down from 26th. Drew Stevens is 9 of 11 on field goals with a long of 57 but has missed three of 11 extra points. Tress Way has put 8 of 25 punts inside the 20 with a 41.7-yard net, Jaylin Lane averages 24.6 yards per kickoff return and Rachaad White 28.1.
